abstract.en: The Mashgiach starts from the Gemara that Mordechai was first counted fourth among the leaders who went up to Eretz Yisroel and later fifth, from which Rav Yosef learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives, and asks how this fits with Mordechai's greatness. He brings the Gemara that Rabbi Meir wrote a Megillah from memory and explains, with the Midrash that Rabbi Meir's Torah read 'garments of light', that Rabbi Meir saw through the outer skin of creation to the Torah inside it, so he copied the Megillah from creation itself. He then brings the eight kings of Edom, where Divrei Hayamim, written by Ezra, says the eighth king died while the Torah does not, and distinguishes, through the Gemara about Moshe and Rabbi Akiva, between seeing with prophecy and understanding with wisdom. From his level of prophecy Ezra did not see Mordechai's inner Torah. So too some of the Sanhedrin, whose portion was the plain meaning, as in the stories of the Beis Yosef and of a student of the Lechovitcher. The majority saw Mordechai's greatness.

en: From Mordechai being counted fourth and later fifth, Rav Yosef learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives.
The world was created through the Torah, so every part of creation is a part of the Torah, and a higher person sees that inner Torah rather than the outer shell.
Rabbi Meir could look through the 'skin' covering creation and see the Torah in it, which is how he could write a Megillah without a written copy.
A prophet sees with his eyes, while a sage understands with wisdom; one can grasp a matter with wisdom without having reached it in prophecy.
While Mordechai worked to save lives he saw the inner Torah of the Megillah's events, so for him it was no loss of Torah study.
Some of the Sanhedrin, whose portion in Torah was its plain meaning, saw it as a loss of Torah study and separated from him, while the majority saw his greatness.

Each year the moon falls further behind the sun, until the leap year, when in Adar Sheni the sun's year and the moon's year are evened out; Adar Rishon is the time of distance.

On Purim Katan the Megillah is read in Heaven, in Rabbi Yosi's yeshivah, and great lights come down that break the concealment of Adar Rishon.
Purim is a new receiving of the Torah and brings a pure desire for Torah, yiras Shamayim and mitzvos.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the test of the last generation before Moshiach is emunah, using the Chafetz Chaim's words after a dibbuk in Radin, and shows how in a time of hester panim the whole world becomes a test of faith.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the generations run in a cycle from Moshe Rabbeinu's generation to the generation before Moshiach, and that we now stand at its end. He explains what a dibbuk is and tells the story of a girl in Radin whose dibbuk Rabbi Elchonon Wasserman drove out as the Chafetz Chaim's messenger. The Chafetz Chaim then said there would be no more dibbukim until Moshiach, because a dibbuk makes emunah easy, and the test of this generation is emunah. The Mashgiach explains why later dibbukim in Eretz Yisrael do not contradict this, and why open wonders of tzaddikim have become rare. Every generation has its own test: for the Noam Elimelech it was tzitzis, as seen in the Divrei Chaim's teshuvos on machine-made tzitzis. Today the Satan is given license in emunah; this is the hester panim the Torah foretold, and Adar and Purim are given to strengthen emunah.

en: The Chafetz Chaim said there would be no more dibbukim until Moshiach, because seeing a dibbuk makes emunah easy, while the test of this generation is emunah.
Every generation has its own test; in the time of the Noam Elimelech it was tzitzis, and today it is emunah.
Open wonders of tzaddikim, once common, have become rare like a flash of lightning in the dark, because Hashem's presence is now veiled.
Since the test of the time is emunah, the Satan has license to entice and trip people up in emunah, and everything a Jew meets today, even the radio and the media, is a test of faith.
This is the hester panim the Torah foretold for the period before Moshiach: Hashem is in every part of creation, but He is not seen.
The months of Adar and Purim were given to strengthen emunah, and the Mashgiach urges holding on to emunah with all one's strength and setting time to learn and practice it.

He turns to the two luminaries: the moon, the 'small luminary', stands for Knesses Yisrael, diminished in its light and in its year of about 355 days against the sun's 365. en: The moon, the 'small luminary', represents Knesses Yisrael, and it was diminished in two ways: in its light and in the length of its year.
Each year the moon falls farther behind the sun, and only in Adar Sheni of a leap year do they line up again, so Adar Rishon is the peak of the distance and the hiddenness.
Although the halacha follows the view that the Megillah is read in Adar Sheni, Rabbi Yosi's view that it is read in Adar Rishon is also true, as 'elu v'elu divrei Elokim chaim'.
In heaven the Megillah is read on Purim Katan in the mesivta of Rabbi Yosi, and the lights that descend break the hester panim of Adar Rishon.
The lights of Purim Katan are doubled and redoubled when Adar Sheni comes.
Purim brings new lights that were never in the world before, not on Shabbos and not on Yom Tov, and on Purim Katan they come down as well.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Esther's words that she had not been called before the king for thirty days, noting that thirty days marks a new period. Citing the Rambam, he explains that one who davens must know he stands before the King, that each word of tefillah is a heichal, and that before every aliyah comes a yeridah. In his first approach, Esther, about to rise to 'vatilbash Esther malchus', felt for thirty days that she could not say a warm word before Hashem; Mordechai answered 'al tedami venafshech', and the Mashgiach compares Avraham sitting at the opening of the tent, who then received the revelation. After a remark on Shushan Purim, his second approach: the thirty days before Pesach were her preparation in purity, and Mordechai told her that her personal preparation must yield to the need of Klal Yisroel. en: Thirty days is a set period of time; after thirty days a new period begins, which is why Esther counted thirty days without being called.
One who davens must know that he stands before the King; each word of tefillah is a heichal, and one goes from one heichal to the next.

Esther felt for thirty days that she could not say a warm word before Hashem and asked how she could bring a yeshuah; Mordechai answered 'al tedami venafshech', not to make calculations about herself.
A descent comes before an ascent and is its preparation, as with Avraham Avinu, who sat at the opening of the tent and precisely then received a great revelation.

In a second approach, the thirty days were the thirty days before Pesach, in which Esther was preparing herself in purity, and Mordechai told her that her personal preparation must yield to the need of Klal Yisroel.
The Mashgiach applies this to the present: looking at the time, one must prepare for a great yeshuah and daven for the klal, not only for oneself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Arizal's words that it is a mitzvah to rejoice in the simcha of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who asked that people rejoice on his hillula. Rashbi was not grasped even by his colleagues, which is why the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda; in the future, when the world is filled with knowledge of Hashem, it will follow Rabbi Shimon. Yet even the lowest Jew has a place at his simcha. The Mashgiach then tells of Rashbi's miracles, above all the valley he filled with golden dinars, and asks why the Midrash calls the taking back of Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta's gift a greater miracle but says nothing of the kind about Rashbi. He answers that the gold was Rashbi's own Torah secrets spread over Meron, which took material form because the students showed interest in wealth; it was no gift from heaven, and when they held back it returned to Torah. He closes with blessings that Rashbi's merit bring the redemption, and with the niggun the Satmar Rav learned in Meron.

en: Following the Arizal and the Zohar, the Mashgiach says it is a mitzvah and a nachas for every Jew to rejoice on the hillula of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.
The halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda rather than Rabbi Shimon because his contemporaries could not grasp him; in the future, when the world is full of knowledge of Hashem, it will follow Rabbi Shimon.
The golden dinars that filled the valley of Meron were Rashbi's chiddushei Torah, which took material form because his students showed interest in wealth.
Since the gold was not sent from heaven but was Torah already present in Meron, its disappearance was no miracle: it simply returned to being Torah.
Rashbi said he could free the whole world from judgment, and the Mashgiach prays that his merit bring the redemption.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that Nitzavim-Vayelech, the sedra of the present century according to the Gra, foretells both the hester panim and destruction of this era and the teshuvah and redemption that follow, with the healing placed before the blow.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the end of the galus as a time of hester panim, in which even the concealment is concealed. He brings the teaching of the Vilna Gaon, recorded by his talmidim, that the sedras of Devarim correspond to the centuries of the sixth millennium, and the Gra's answer to Reb Chaim of Volozhin that he himself is the 'even shleimah' of Ki Seitzei. Since Nitzavim and Vayelech count as one sedra, they hold the events of the century that began in 5700. He tells how, as a boy in 1939, he saw the shul weep on Rosh Hashanah while the boys trusted the radio that Germany would fall in days. Vayelech foretells the hester panim; Nitzavim foretells the teshuvah and ingathering. Nitzavim comes first because Hashem prepares the refuah before the makah, and they are two sedras because galus and geulah are two different programs. He closes with today's hester panim and a call to teshuvah.

en: According to the Gra, each sedra of Devarim corresponds to a century of the sixth millennium, and the Gra found himself in Ki Seitzei in the words 'even shleimah', Eliyahu ben Shlomo.
Nitzavim and Vayelech count as one sedra, as the Masorah shows and as answers the Zohar's count of 53 sedras, so they are the sedra of the present century.
Vayelech foretells the hester panim and the tragedy of the Tav-Shin years, and Nitzavim foretells the teshuvah, the ingathering and the return to Eretz Yisrael.
Nitzavim's consolation comes before Vayelech's suffering because with the Jewish people Hashem prepares the refuah before the makah, as a surgeon does.
Galus and geulah fall in one century but cannot share one sedra, because a sedra is a 'program' and the world after Moshiach will run on an entirely new order.
The Mashgiach describes the present as hester panim, with rising antisemitism and 'Haman becoming powerful', and says Hashem wants to arouse the Jewish people to teshuvah.

title.en: The refuah before the makah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the consolation of Nitzavim comes before the suffering of Vayelech, and why one sedra is split in two. He answers the first from the Gemara that Hashem prepares the refuah before the makah for the Jewish people, as in the Megillah, and explains it with the difference between a murderer and a surgeon.

title.en: A sedra is a program

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a sedra is a 'program' that tells what is happening, and tells how the Maggid of Mezritch chose the future Ba'al HaTanya as his baal korei. Since the world after Moshiach will run on a new order, galus and geulah cannot be in one sedra.

title.en: Today's hester panim and the call to teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the story of Esther is alluded to in the Torah's hester panim and compares the Jews' fall in the days of Achashverosh to today. He points to rising antisemitism in Austria and America and closes that Hashem wants to stir the Jewish people to teshuvah, with a wish for the consolations of this century.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to children on Lag BaOmer, the Mashgiach teaches that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai brought friendship into the world, and that when Jewish children are friends, learn Torah and daven, Moshiach comes and even the wild animals become friends of the Jews.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks the children whether they want to hear what will be when Moshiach comes, and describes the prophecy of Yeshayahu: the wolf, tiger and lion will live in peace with the lamb, the kid and the calf, and nothing will harm anyone. He then explains Lag BaOmer: Rabbi Akiva's students died because they were not good friends to one another, but through Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai peace came among the students. When Jewish children are friends and help each other, Moshiach comes and the animals too become friends of the Jews. Jews today need a great salvation from enemies who surround them, and the custom of shooting bow and arrow on Lag BaOmer recalls Yaakov Avinu's sword and bow, which Onkelos renders as his tefillos. The Mashgiach tells the children that Rabbi Shimon is present and blesses them, and leads them in saying Shema Yisrael.

en: When Moshiach comes, as Yeshayahu prophesies, the wild animals will live in peace with the gentle ones and nothing will harm anyone.
Rabbi Akiva's students died because they were not good friends to one another.
On Lag BaOmer, through Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, peace and friendship came into the world.
When Jewish children are friends with one another, Moshiach comes and even the animals become friends of the Jews.
The bow and arrow of Lag BaOmer stand for Torah and tefillah, like Yaakov Avinu's bow, which Onkelos renders as his tefillos.

title.en: Moshiach, the animals and Rashbi's friendship

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes to the children Yeshayahu's prophecy of peace among the animals when Moshiach comes, then explains that Rabbi Akiva's students died for lack of friendship and that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai brought peace among them. When Jewish children are friends, he says, Moshiach comes and the animals become friends too.

title.en: The bow of Torah and tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Jews need a great salvation from the enemies around them, explains the Lag BaOmer custom of bow and arrow through Yaakov Avinu's bow, which Onkelos renders as tefillah, and tells the children that Rabbi Shimon is present and blesses them. He leads them in Shema Yisrael and prays for Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah is the yom tov of hod, thanking and praising Hashem out of a feeling that nothing is owed to oneself, and that this middah must be taken from Chanukah for the whole year by thanking Hashem for every small thing.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by tying the nights of Chanukah to the middos and says Chanukah is the yom tov of hod. He brings the Lubavitcher Rebbe's observation that on the fifth night Beis Hillel's count first exceeds Beis Shammai's, and the Ramban that the Chanukah lights of Aharon's descendants are Aharon's lasting share. Hod means both admitting and praising, and the two are one: only someone who feels nothing is owed him can truly thank, as Aharon rejoiced when Moshe was chosen. The Jewish day, davening and Shabbos all open with thanks; Yehudah, named for thanks, and Matisyahu, a spark of Yehudah, set Chanukah for praise. In the future only the korban todah remains, so one must learn here to delight in praise, above all on Shabbos and through song. He tells of a camp survivor saved by stolen bread, speaks of the hundred berachos, and reads a tzaddik's will thanking Hashem for every small thing.

en: Chanukah is the yom tov of the middah of hod, and the fifth night, the night of hod, was especially cherished by tzaddikim.
Hod means both admitting and praising, and both come from shiflus: only one who feels nothing is owed to him can thank with his whole heart.
The Jewish day begins with Modeh Ani, davening begins with Hodu and Mizmor l'Todah, and Shabbos begins with Tov l'hodos: thanks is the beginning that includes everything.
In the future only the korban todah will remain, so a person must accustom himself here, above all on Shabbos, to delight in praising Hashem.
Each yom tov's middah is meant for the whole year, and from Chanukah one draws hod: thanking Hashem for every small thing, even for what is not good.
Thanking Hashem for every detail rests on emunah in hashgacha pratis, and the Mashgiach says anyone can get used to it without being a great baal madreigah.

title.en: Hod: admitting and praising, from shiflus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the two meanings of hod, admitting and praising, and shows they are one: only a person who feels nothing is owed him can thank fully. Aharon, who rejoiced in his heart when his younger brother Moshe was chosen, is the model of this hod.

title.en: Everything begins with thanks

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the Jewish day opens with Modeh Ani, the davening with Hodu and Mizmor l'Todah, and Shabbos with Tov l'hodos. Yehudah, named for thanks, leads the degalim, and Matisyahu, a spark of Yehudah, and his beis din set Chanukah to thank and praise.

title.en: Thanks in the future, Shabbos and song

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Kedushas Levi that pesukei d'zimra is the core of davening, and that in the future all korbanos cease except the todah. One must learn here to delight in praise; Shabbos, a taste of the World to Come, is the time for it, and song, which the Zohar places above letters and vowels, raises it higher.

title.en: Learning to thank for every small thing

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes the extra mizmorim of Shabbos and says anyone can train himself to praise Hashem for every small thing, looking at the beauty of the world He made. He adds that one can find chesed within din, as people tell how good came out of something bad.

title.en: The stolen bread in the camp

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Jew in a Nazi camp at the end of the war whose extra pieces of bread were stolen by Russian prisoners who beat him; in the morning the thieves lay dead, because the Nazis had poisoned the bread. He brings it as an example of good growing out of something bad.

title.en: The hundred berachos and saying them from a siddur

summary.en: The Mashgiach recounts that David HaMelech instituted a hundred berachos a day when a hundred people were dying daily because Hashem was not praised enough, and that the decree still stands. He encourages saying berachos with kavanah from a siddur, and hanging Asher Yatzar by the sink.

title.en: Taking hod from Chanukah for the whole year

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each yom tov's middah is for the whole year, as Pesach's freedom and Shavuos's Torah, and Chanukah is the wellspring of hod. Most of Tehillim is praise, and praise draws further salvations; he brings a tzaddik praised by the Rebbe of Lublin, who told his children he had thanked Hashem for everything, even the unwanted.

title.en: The tzaddik's thanks and the closing wish

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads from the tzaddik's will how he thanked Hashem for a private room, for his Shabbos clothes, for a snuff box that fell without opening and glasses that fell without breaking, out of emunah that everything comes from Hashem. He closes that one should take this hod from Chanukah, thank for everything, and get used to it, and wishes for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach reads the lean cows in Pharaoh's dream standing in astonishment beside the fat ones as the sitra achra, and Hashem Himself, marveling at the Jewish soul's mesiras nefesh, seen at Chanukah, in the Alter Rebbe and the Rebbes of Lubavitch, and in the shluchim of today.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why the lean cows in Pharaoh's dream first stood beside the fat ones before swallowing them, and why Pharaoh left this out when he retold the dream. With Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch's reading of 'our feet stood in your gates, Yerushalayim' he explains standing as being frozen in wonder. The fat cows are the G-dly soul with its seven holy middos, the lean ones the animal soul; even when the holy soul seems swallowed, the sitra achra stands amazed before it, and Hashem Himself marvels, as the Gemara brings from Zechariah. Pharaoh, ashamed, hid this. At Chanukah the Jews felt the loss of Torah as a true tzarah and gave their lives, and so the Rambam calls the mitzvah very dear, like Avraham's milah that came through pain. The Mashgiach ends with the mesiras nefesh of the Alter Rebbe, the Lubavitcher Rebbes and the shluchim.

en: The fat cows are the G-dly soul with its seven holy middos, and the lean cows are the animal soul with its seven middos, which can swallow the holy soul into exile.
The lean cows' standing is the sitra achra stopping in astonishment before the greatness of a Jewish soul, which it cannot truly swallow.
Hashem Himself marvels at how Jews withstood the exile, as the Gemara brings from the passuk in Zechariah 'it will also be wondrous in My eyes'.
Pharaoh left the standing out of his retelling out of shame, and his claim that the swallowed cows could not be recognized is a lie: the Jewish soul remains and acts.

At Chanukah the Jews felt the loss of Torah and mitzvos as a real tzarah and gave their lives for it; therefore the Rambam calls Chanukah a very dear mitzvah, as a mitzvah that comes through pain is dear.
The Alter Rebbe and all the Rebbes of Lubavitch gave their lives for Chassidus, and the last Rebbe's shluchim continue that mesiras nefesh, at which the world and Hashem marvel.

title.en: Why the lean cows stood still

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the starving cows in Pharaoh's dream stood beside the fat ones instead of swallowing them at once, and why Pharaoh omitted this when retelling the dream. He brings Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch's explanation that 'our feet stood in your gates, Yerushalayim' means being frozen in awe.

title.en: The animal soul stands amazed

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the fat cows as the G-dly soul and the lean ones as the animal soul, and says that the sitra achra, and Hashem Himself as the Gemara brings from Zechariah, marvel at the Jewish soul surviving in exile. Pharaoh hid this out of shame and falsely claimed the swallowed cows left no trace.

title.en: Chanukah: a tzarah only Jews feel

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Greeks' decrees against Torah: a gentile wonders what kind of tzarah that is, but for Jews it was a true tzarah, and they gave their lives, so Hashem marveled and brought the salvation and the Chanukah lights. He explains the Rambam's 'very dear mitzvah' through Rashi on Avraham's oath by the milah, which came through pain.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh of Lubavitch and the shluchim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Alter Rebbe and all the Lubavitcher Rebbes giving their lives for Chassidus, the Rayatz demanding mesiras nefesh of his chassidim, and the last Rebbe's shluchim, four thousand of whom were recently photographed at 770. The world and Hashem marvel, and he closes with a wish for the Geulah, when the world will marvel at how Jews endured the exile.

catalogTitle: Purim - Hashem Behind the Cloak of עשו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the miracles of Purim and Adar are real but hidden, cloaked by the concealment of Amalek, and that the Megillah trains a Jew to find Hashem's name behind the cloak of nature.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the greatness of Purim: the Arizal places it above every Yom Tov, and the Chasam Sofer says the kedushah of the Megillah exceeds that of the anointing oil. Adar is the heel of the year, farthest from Nissan, and it matches the lowest souls of Klal Yisrael, the ones Amalek attacked when the clouds of glory rejected them. Every Jew still keeps a hidden point of love for Hashem, and so the Purim miracle came even for sinners; at the very feast they wrongly enjoyed, Hashem removed Vashti to make room for Esther. Nissan holds revealed miracles, Adar hidden ones, as the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of the dying patient shows. The Megillah has no open miracle and no name of Hashem because Amalek conceals Him, yet His name is hidden at its turning points. The Megillah teaches a Jew to read Hashem's plan in world events and in his own life.

en: Adar, the last month and farthest from Nissan, corresponds to the lowest souls of Klal Yisrael, and the Purim miracle was given even for those who had sinned.
Every Jew, even a great rasha, has a hidden point inherited from the Avos where he wants to be good, and so Hashem's love for him remains.
Nissan is the month of revealed miracles, while the miracles of Adar are hidden, cloaked in nature.
The Megillah shows no open miracle and does not mention Hashem's name because Amalek's concealment hides Hashem.
The Megillah is an exercise in finding Hashem's name hidden in whatever happens in the world and in one's own life.

title.en: Purim, the heel of the year, and Hashem's love

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the greatness of Purim, citing the Arizal and the Chasam Sofer, and explains that Adar, the heel of the year, matches the lowest souls whom Amalek attacked. Since every Jew keeps a hidden love for Hashem, the Purim miracle came even for sinners, prepared at the very feast of Achashverosh, like a father's mercy described in Parshas Ki Sisa.

title.en: Revealed miracles and hidden miracles

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Nissan, the month of open miracles, with Adar, where the Megillah reads like a story without miracles and without Hashem's name. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of a dying patient whose distant doctor and medicine arrive just in time, showing Hashem's hidden hand.

title.en: Every step of the Megillah is part of the miracle

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows how each event in the Megillah happens just in time and fits a plan, and says a person who examines his own day would see miracles in it too. Adar is named for the aderes, a cloak: its miracles are cloaked in nature. He then asks why the Megillah shows no miracles.

title.en: Amalek hides Hashem's name

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that Amalek conceals Hashem, as Rashi explains that Hashem's name and throne are incomplete because of Amalek. In the Megillah Hashem is hidden in the word HaMelech, which, like kes Kah and Haman, equals 95; Achashverosh is a puppet on Hashem's strings, and Hashem's name is hidden at the Megillah's turning points.

title.en: Learning to read the hidden plan

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that the Megillah is an exercise in finding Hashem's name in everything that happens, like a trained doctor reading an X-ray or a reader seeing a master plan in the newspaper. Like a masked Purim visitor, the world is only a shroud with Hashem underneath, and a person who looks into the events of his life will see miracles.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the light of Shabbos, which lifts souls upward, with the light of Chanukah, which descends to the lowest places, and sees in this the path of the Chabad Rebbes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the pairs Hashem set in the world, holiness against its opposite, light against darkness, day against night, inside against outside, and notes that the Chanukah light belongs to night, darkness and the public domain. He brings the Midrash of Yaakov's ladder, where Yaakov saw the angels of the kingdoms rise and fall and Edom rise without end, and asks how the Midrash can say Yaakov did not believe. He contrasts the Shabbos light, which raises a Jew upward, with the Chanukah light, which can kindle even the 'disqualified oils'. Yaakov is the aspect of Shabbos, but some souls bound to him cannot hold on to it; for their sake Yaakov asked that the Shechinah come down below ten, and this became Chanukah. The Mashgiach applies this to the Alter Rebbe, who raised his chassidim, and to the later Chabad Rebbes, who went down to the lowest places.

en: The Chanukah light belongs to the side of night, darkness and the public domain, unlike the Menorah of the Beis HaMikdash.
Shabbos is the highest point in time and lifts a Jew upward, but some fallen souls cannot hold on to it.
What Shabbos cannot kindle, Chanukah can: the 'disqualified oils' not lit on Shabbos are lit on Chanukah.
For the sake of the souls who cannot rise with him, Yaakov asked that the Shechinah come down to them, below ten, and from this came Chanukah.
The Alter Rebbe lifted his chassidim upward, like Shabbos, while the later Chabad Rebbes went down with the Chanukah light to the lowest places to raise Jews.

title.en: Chanukah's light and Yaakov's ladder

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the pairs of holiness and its opposite and shows that the Chanukah light belongs to night, darkness and the outside. He brings the Midrash of Yaakov's ladder and the angels of the kingdoms, and asks how the Midrash can say that Yaakov, the root of bitachon, did not believe.

title.en: The Shabbos light and the Chanukah light

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the Shabbos candle, inside and above ten, with the Chanukah candle, outside and below ten, and brings the Me'or Einayim that the oils not lit on Shabbos are lit on Chanukah. He explains that Yaakov is the aspect of Shabbos, the trunk from which the twelve tribes branch out, and that some fallen souls cannot hold on to Shabbos to rise with it.

title.en: Yaakov's plea brings down the Shechinah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yaakov saw the souls bound to him that had fallen to the side of Esav and could not believe, and that this is the meaning of the Midrash's 'he did not believe'. Yaakov refused to go up alone and asked that the Shechinah come down below ten; 'Hashem stood over him', and Hashem promised there would be a Chanukah.

title.en: The Alter Rebbe's Shabbos and Chabad's Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Alter Rebbe raised his chassidim to lofty levels, and tells of Reb Avraham Zuskin, whom he saw davening on Shabbos with tears for hours. He then says the later Chabad Rebbes did the opposite, going down with the Chanukah light through shluchim to Jews with no Jewish education, and closes with a tefillah that Jews spread chassidus and be redeemed.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Alter Rebbe, by writing the title page of the Tanya himself, went out like the Chanukah light to the doorway outside, to call to the Jews who are far that Hashem is close to them.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by recalling that his rebbe in Mesivta Torah Vodaath, Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, chose the Tanya out of all seforim to learn with his talmidim, and that he follows that example. He points to a detail of the Tanya: the Alter Rebbe wrote its title page himself, built on the passuk "ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od", and Chabad learns it as part of the sefer. To explain this he turns to Chanukah: unlike Shabbos and Yom Tov, when a Jew rises upward, on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down below ten tefachim, into the reshus harabim, on a weekday. So too the Alter Rebbe goes out to the doorway, the title page, and calls to weekday Jews that they are close to Hashem. Today, when hidden wisdom opens for the nations, Jewish youth need the Tanya and the inner Torah. He ends with the nesi'im read on Chanukah, the light of Moshiach in the Chanukah candles, and a tefillah.

en: The Alter Rebbe wrote the title page of the Tanya himself, on the passuk "ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od", and Chabad learns it as part of the sefer; the Mashgiach says this detail mirrors the whole path of Chabad.
Unlike Shabbos and Yom Tov, when one rises up to holiness, on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down below ten tefachim, to the reshus harabim, on a weekday, to light up and warm Jews who are far.
The Alter Rebbe does not wait for Jews to come in; through the title page he goes out to the doorway and calls to weekday Jews that they are close to Hashem and should come inside.
Today, more than in earlier times, the Tanya is needed for the youth, so that the wisdom now being revealed to the nations should not dim the light of the Torah's depths.
On Chanukah one reads the parshah of the nesi'im, whose korbanos counter the kelipah of Yishmael, and one should set times to learn pnimiyus haTorah, the hidden light of Moshiach.

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Chanukah, unlike Shabbos and Yom Tov, the Shechinah comes down below ten tefachim, outside into the reshus harabim on a weekday, and brings the Chiddushei HaRim that Chanukah and Purim are weekday yomim tovim that sustain Jews in galus. title.en: Why the youth need the Tanya today

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Tanya's yom tov falls in Kislev, the month of Chanukah, and that both go outside, like Moshe Rabbeinu calling "mi laShem eilai" at the gate of the camp. He says that today, when hidden wisdom opens for the nations, Jewish youth need the Tanya, the Torah of Moshiach, so that outside wisdom does not dim the light of the Torah and of the soul's hidden depths.

title.en: The nesi'im, the hidden light and a tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the parshah of the nesi'im read on Chanukah counters the kelipah of Yishmael, as the Zohar says, a yeshuah needed today for Jews in Eretz Yisroel. He calls for set times to learn pnimiyus haTorah, the hidden light of Moshiach revealed by the Chanukah candles as the Bnei Yissaschar brings, and closes with a tefillah in the merit of the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Maggid and the Ba'al HaTanya.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows how the light of Moshiach hidden in the darkness of Parshas Vayeshev and in the Chanukah lights was revealed through the Ba'al Shem Tov, whose love for every Jew uncovers the hidden light in even the lowest Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the darkness of Parshas Vayeshev: the tribes were busy with the sale of Yosef, Reuven with his sackcloth, Yaakov with his mourning and Yehuda with taking a wife, while Hashem, as the Midrash says, was busy creating the light of Moshiach. Chanukah too holds the hidden light, and the passuk that opens the story of Yehuda equals in gematria 'the king Moshiach ben David'. He then turns to the three hundred years of the Ba'al Shem Tov, the first sparkling of Moshiach, and to the Besht's pipe whose sparks became the many paths of Chassidus. The Besht taught love of Hashem, of the Torah and of Israel, and Chabad carried that love to Jews across the world. The Chozeh of Lublin's words about an informer who had lit Chanukah candles show that the hidden light shines even in the worst Jew. He closes with ahavas Yisrael and a brachah for the full redemption.

en: While the tribes, Reuven, Yaakov and Yehuda were each occupied with the darkness of the sale of Yosef, Hashem was creating the light of Moshiach.
Chanukah is the time of the hidden light, and the Chanukah lights hold the light of the king Moshiach.
The Ba'al Shem Tov was the beginning of the sparkling of Moshiach, and the sparks of his pipe became the many paths of Chassidus that saved the world.
The Besht taught love of Hashem, love of the Torah and love of Israel, which means loving a Jew at the other end of the world whom one never knew.
Chabad carried this love to Jews across the world, sending emissaries to revive them with the spark of Chassidus and Yiddishkeit.
Even the worst Jew holds the hidden light, which the Chanukah lights reveal, and the Besht unites all Jews at the level of yechidah.

summary.en: On the three hundred years of the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Mashgiach explains that the Besht was the beginning of the sparkling of Moshiach, brings the gematria of 'Yisrael Ba'al Shem Tov' and the greatness of Moshiach's soul, and quotes a letter of Rabbi Mendel of Vitebsk. He tells of the sparks of the Besht's pipe that each talmid caught.

title.en: Ahavas Yisrael and how Chabad spread it

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows how the Besht's influence reached the whole world, from the three niggunim of the Besht, the Maggid and the Ba'al HaTanya to the Besht's love of Hashem, the Torah and Israel. He describes how Chabad sent emissaries to Jews everywhere, how the Ba'al HaTanya's Shulchan Aruch and Tanya spread his sparks, and that even the worst rasha holds a point that is no rasha.

title.en: The Chozeh of Lublin and the informer's Chanukah lights

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the story, brought by the Imrei Emes, of the Chozeh of Lublin, who would not curse an informer on the night he lit Chanukah candles because he then shone in all worlds. He explains that the Chanukah lights reveal the hidden light in every Jew, brings the Pri Tzaddik, and closes with the Besht's ahavas Yisrael and a brachah for the full redemption.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Akeidah was Avraham Avinu's hardest test because he saw Hashem only 'from a distance', confused by questions he could not answer, and that Klal Yisrael at the end of the golus is living through that same tenth test.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Parshas HaAkeidah, said every morning, and asks why the last of Avraham's ten tests was the hardest. He contrasts it with the first test, Ur Kasdim, where Avraham, searching for the truth, gave his life for a Creator he had never seen. A test, he explains from the double meaning of nisayon, is meant to raise a person, so each one is harder than the last. The Zohar points to 'he saw the place from a distance': at the Akeidah Avraham felt far from Hashem, because the command contradicted the promise that his seed would come from Yitzchak, and kashyos about Hashem's truth entered his mind. He pushed them away and went blindly. Why he did not notice that he was only told to bring Yitzchak up, as Rashi explains, is answered: when Hashem does not want a person to know, he does not know, as with Haman and the seventh of Adar. Following the Ramban that the fathers' events foreshadow the children's, the Mashgiach says Klal Yisrael now faces the tenth test of hester panim and must hold on to emunah.

en: The Akeidah, the tenth and last of Avraham's tests, was the hardest; had he failed it, the Mashgiach says, all the earlier tests would have been lost.
A nisayon is also a raising, like a flag (nes) held high: every test is meant to promote a person, so each test is harder than the one before.
At the Akeidah Avraham saw Hashem 'from a distance': the command to slaughter Yitzchak seemed to contradict the promise that his seed would come through Yitzchak, and kashyos made him feel estranged.
Avraham dismissed the kashyos, covered his eyes, said Shema Yisrael and went to the Akeidah blindly, without giving the questions any place in his mind.
When Hashem does not want a person to know something, even the wisest cannot figure it out; so it was with Avraham at the Akeidah and with Haman and the seventh of Adar.

Following the Ramban that the fathers' events foreshadow the children's, Klal Yisrael at the end of the golus is going through Avraham's tenth test of hester panim, and those who hold on to emunah will pass it.

title.en: The Akeidah: the hardest of the ten tests

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Parshas HaAkeidah, said every morning, and asks why it is the climax of tefillah. He asks who in the room would not obey if Hashem appeared and commanded him, and notes that Avraham passed all ten tests, the Akeidah being the last and hardest.

title.en: The first test: Ur Kasdim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how young Avraham searched for the truth, rejected the sun and the moon, concluded there is one Creator, defied Nimrod and was thrown into the fire unharmed. Hashem then revealed Himself to him, but in Ur Kasdim Avraham gave his life for a G-d he had never seen.

title.en: Nisayon means raising; seeing Hashem from afar

summary.en: From lashon hakodesh, where nisayon also means raising, the Mashgiach explains that every test is meant to promote, so each is harder than the last. He then asks why the Akeidah was harder than Ur Kasdim and brings the Zohar's hint: 'he saw the Place from a distance', echoed in the haftarah of the second day of Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Avraham's confusion and his blind faith

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Avraham's inner turmoil: Hashem is Emes and keeps His word, yet the command to slaughter Yitzchak contradicted the promise of seed through him. Avraham pushed the kashyos away, covered his eyes and said Shema, and went blindly; afterwards he asked the malach why Hashem had changed His mind, and was told, as Rashi brings, that he was only told to bring Yitzchak up.

title.en: When Hashem hides, one does not know

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how Avraham, who understood Hashem more than the malachim, missed what a child learning Rashi sees, and answers that when Hashem tests a person and does not want him to know, he does not know. He applies the same answer to Haman, who calculated that Moshe died on the seventh of Adar but did not realize he was also born then.

title.en: Maaseh avos siman labanim: the tenth test today

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the Akeidah a test of hester panim and brings the Ramban in Lech Lecha that the fathers' events foreshadow the children's: the famine, Pharaoh taking Sarah, the plagues and the gifts. By that pattern Klal Yisrael goes through Avraham's ten tests, and at the end of the golus faces the tenth: a whole world full of kashyos, from the Holocaust to the darkness of most of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Holding on to emunah until Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls books written after the war questioning Hashem, and says that today a handful of Yidden who believe are living through Avraham's last test, with the promise that emunah will prevail. Like Avraham, one must cover one's eyes and say Shema and 'Hashem Elokeichem Emes'; the added word Emes corresponds to the 'eikev', the heels of Moshiach, which is why Avraham was told 'eikev asher shamata bekoli'.

oneLiner.en: For Yud-Tes Kislev, the Mashgiach explains the Midrash that Eisav will return Yaakov's gift in the days of Moshiach as the return of Jewish souls held captive, and shows how the lights of Shabbos and Chanukah and the hidden light of pnimiyus haTorah bring them back.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the tradition that on Chanukah the hidden light of the six days of creation is revealed, and that the Alter Rebbe's name Shneur means two lights, of the revealed and the hidden Torah, a thread that ran through all the Chabad Rebbes. He links this to the Gemara that one who is careful with ner Shabbos and ner Chanukah merits sons who are talmidei chachamim, and to the Lubavitcher Rebbe's campaigns for both lights. He then brings the Midrash of an am ha'aretz who told Rabbi Hoshaya that Eisav will return Yaakov's gift when Moshiach comes, and asks why this was revealed to an am ha'aretz and why 580 animals matter. Yaakov's sheep are Jewish souls; the blemished animals given to Eisav are souls left under his rule, and the story of Dina and Osnas shows what Yaakov invested. Yud-Tes Kislev, Binyamin's month of Kislev and the study of pnimiyus haTorah bring them back, and he closes on the year 5760 and the eight Chanukah lights.

en: The Alter Rebbe's name Shneur means two lights, the light of the revealed Torah and of the hidden Torah, and this inner thread passed through every generation of the Chabad Rebbes.
Ner Shabbos and ner Chanukah are the two lights the Lubavitcher Rebbe spread, and through them he brought Jews in the lowest places back to their Father in Heaven.
Yaakov's sheep are Jewish souls, and the animals of his gift to Eisav are souls that remained under Eisav's rule; when Moshiach comes Eisav must give them back.
The am ha'aretz grasped 'mincha yashiv' because the root of his own soul was in the parsha of Yaakov's gift, and he sensed that he would return to his root.
Kislev is the month of pnimiyus haTorah, and the redemption is to come through it; on Yud-Tes Kislev many thousands begin learning Tanya.
Against the 'klipah of 2000' in the year 5760, the Mashgiach sets the eight lights of Chanukah, since eight times 'ner' equals 2000.

title.en: The angel's touch and the blemished animals

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yaakov's encounter with Eisav's angel foreshadowed his meeting with Eisav, and that the angel's touch left spiritual blemishes among Yaakov's children. The animals sent to Eisav were blemished, and giving them up was an investment.

title.en: Dina, Osnas and Moshiach ben Yosef

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Osnas, Yosef's wife, was Dina's daughter from Shechem, and explains with gematrios that a spark of Moshiach ben Yosef was hidden in Shechem. Yaakov knew this secret and kept silent, and already at Dina's birth, as Rashi says, she was meant to be a son.

title.en: Every Jew a letter: the am ha'aretz's root

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Midrash: Jewish souls are held by Eisav because of the gift, every Jew has a letter in a parsha of the Torah, and the am ha'aretz felt his root was in the parsha of the gift. He then describes the Rebbe's work of rescuing souls through ner Chanukah, which reaches below ten tefachim, and ner Shabbos, which raises even little girls.

title.en: Yud-Tes Kislev, Binyamin and pnimiyus haTorah

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives a gematria for Yud-Tes Kislev, explains Yaakov's answer to Eisav through the two lights hinted in 'the children whom G-d graciously gave', and ties Binyamin's separate blessing of chanina to Kislev and Chanukah. He then explains that the Alter Rebbe began the 'mincha yashiv', and that the redemption comes through pnimiyus haTorah, revealed in Kislev.

title.en: The year 5760 and the eight Chanukah lights

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the year 5760 as a time suited for redemption and of the missionary effort he calls the 'klipah of 2000', set against Chabad's work of bringing Jews back. Eight times 'ner' equals 2000, and he closes with taking on the study of pnimiyus haTorah and a wish for Moshiach. Another speaker then thanks him.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that because the highest sparks fell lowest, the lowly generation before Moshiach has the task of the Chanukah light: to go down into the darkest places and raise them, as the Lubavitcher Rebbe taught.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that every leader of Israel guides those bound to him, but the Lubavitcher Rebbe made a revolution in the whole world. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya's principle on parshas Vayishlach that the higher a thing is, the lower it falls: Esav came from the world of tohu, higher than Yaakov, and fell lowest. This encourages our low generation, the heels of Moshiach: great souls lie deep in the kelipos, and only a generation that is itself low can raise them, as a story about lokshen at the bottom of a plate shows. Chanukah, lit below ten tefachim in the public domain, expresses this. He traces the Kislev parshiyos as descents to bring out holiness, explains how Lavan's blessing to Eliezer was meant for his bad side and was turned to good, and how the tefillah of Moshiach is hidden in Lavan's blessing to Rivka. He ends with the Rebbe's shluchim, a Chanukah light that still shines, and the call to ask for Moshiach.

en: Following the Ba'al HaTanya, the higher a thing is, the lower it falls: Esav, from the world of tohu, stood higher than Yaakov and fell lower.
Our low generation, the heels of Moshiach, can raise great souls lying deep in the kelipos that earlier, holier generations could not reach.
Chanukah is the mitzvah of going out of the private domain into the public domain and lighting below ten tefachim.
The Kislev parshiyos all tell of going down into a low place to bring out holiness: Rivka from Charan, the brachos from Esav, the shevatim, Osnas and Peretz.
Lavan blessed Eliezer meaning to strengthen his bad side, but Hashem turned the blessing to good.
The Lubavitcher Rebbe lit a Chanukah light in the world through his shluchim and taught Jews to ask for Moshiach.

He calls this a great encouragement for our generation.

title.en: The Kislev parshiyos: going down to raise sparks

summary.en: The Mashgiach traces the parshiyos read in Kislev: Eliezer brings Rivka out of Charan, Yaakov goes into the place of falsehood to take the brachos of Moshiach from Esav, then Rachel and Leah, Osnas, and Peretz. He adds that Eliezer himself went from cursed to blessed through Lavan's words.

title.en: Why Lavan blessed Eliezer

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal's answer that Eliezer had a good part and a bad part, Og king of Bashan, and asks why Lavan, who is Bilaam, would bless him. He explains that Lavan meant to strengthen the bad part, but as with Bilaam, Hashem turned the curse into a blessing.

title.en: Avraham's prayer for Yishmael and the prayer of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar's complaint that Avraham prayed for Yishmael and not for us, and answers with the prayer of Moshiach, who is greater than Avraham. He shows how Lavan's blessing to Rivka was aimed at Yishmael, but Hashem placed in it the prayer of Moshiach.

title.en: The Chanukah light in the public domain

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Lavan's anger at Eliezer for coming into his territory to take out Rivka's soul, a Chanukah light lit outside. He says this is our generation's task, which the Lubavitcher Rebbe showed through his shluchim and his call to ask for Moshiach, and closes with a blessing in the merit of the Ba'al HaTanya.

oneLiner.en: For Yud-Tes Kislev the Mashgiach explains that the Alter Rebbe's release, 'Padah beshalom nafshi', is a call for peace among Jews, and that only shalom, the inner meaning of Chanukah, can subdue Yishmael, the 'hater of peace'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Alter Rebbe's letter 'Katonti', written after his release from Petersburg, in which he asks his chassidim to stay humble and not to bear a grudge against their opponents, but to answer them with love. Yud-Tes Kislev is a 'day of tidings', and the tiding is peace: the release came as the Alter Rebbe said 'Padah beshalom nafshi'. The Mashgiach then brings the Zohar and Targum Yonasan that the offerings of the twelve nesiim at the dedication of the Mizbe'ach subdue the twelve princes of Yishmael. Yishmael, he explains with the Rambam and the pesukim of Tehillim, is the 'hater of peace' and a 'pere adam', as the Chofetz Chaim once said. The nesiim stood for unity, and Chanukah, the yom tov of hod and of Yosef, is peace: shalom bayis outweighs the Chanukah light, the menorah is one piece. He ends that every Jew must take stock of his own love of peace, which alone defeats the hater of peace.

en: In the letter 'Katonti' the Alter Rebbe asks his chassidim to stay humble and to meet their opponents with love rather than resentment.
The Alter Rebbe's release came as he said 'Padah beshalom nafshi', and he took it to mean that his redemption should bring peace among Jews.
The essence of Yishmael is that he hates peace: he is a 'pere adam' who cannot be fought and will not make peace.
The twelve nesiim subdue Yishmael's twelve princes through their unity at the dedication of the Mizbe'ach.
Chanukah is the yom tov of peace, which is why shalom bayis takes precedence over the Chanukah light.
Every Jew must take stock of his middah of shalom, since only love of peace can defeat the hater of peace.

title.en: Chanukah, Yosef and peace against Yishmael

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Chanukah is peace: the menorah is made of one piece, the Mizbe'ach makes peace, and the Chanukah lights subdue the hater of peace. He brings Tanya chapter 32 on loving a fellow Jew, explains that Yosef is the aspect of peace, and that the sale of Yosef to the Yishmaelim still awaits the revenge of Pinchas, who is Eliyahu.

title.en: A reckoning on peace, and blessings

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Satan, sensing his end as Moshiach approaches, fights emunah with all his strength, and that after failing to 'bite' the Jews through persecution, Esav now 'bites with a kiss' through friendliness, assimilation and the invasion of the Jewish home.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that every person and every generation has a mitzvah of its own, and that in the generation before Moshiach that mitzvah is emunah, as Chavakuk established all the mitzvos on emunah. Because the Satan opposes whatever mitzvah is a person's success, the world today is a battlefield against emunah, just as in Mitzrayim the Jews first believed Moshe and then lost faith when the slavery grew harder. A being in mortal danger fights with new strength, like a dying candle that flares up; the Satan, who will be removed when Moshiach comes, is gasping for life. The Tosfos Yom Tov explains that it was a miracle the Kohen Gadol stayed tahor because the Satan concentrated on him alone. The Sfas Emes explains that Esav, unable to bite Yaakov, 'bit him with a kiss'. The Mashgiach applies this to the Church's new friendliness, to assimilation, and to the Satan's 'last wish': entering the Jewish home through the internet, newspapers and television.

en: Every generation has a mitzvah of its own, and in the generation before the Geulah it is emunah.
The Satan opposes whatever mitzvah is a person's main success, so today the whole world is a battlefield against emunah.
Because the Satan will be removed when Moshiach comes, he fights now with the desperate strength of a dying being, like a candle that flares up before it goes out.
Esav, unable to destroy the Jews by persecution, now 'bites with a kiss' through friendliness and assimilation, which does more damage than the persecution did.
The Satan has been granted a 'last wish' to pass the mezuzah, and he now enters the Jewish home through the internet, newspapers and television.

He closes that one must guard what one reads and sees and will discuss next week how to keep emunah.

abstract.en: After an introduction by the host, the Mashgiach says that the privilege is to take part in the 19 Kislev celebration, and that this year he will only say a few words of brachah. He links 19 Kislev to Chanukah, since it falls in Chanukah's week, and asks a question: the poskim say empty vessels are removed from the table before Birkas Hamazon because a brachah does not rest on emptiness, so why is the brachah on Chanukah made over a menorah whose holders mostly stand empty? He then praises how Chabad enriched the Jewish people, and with a parable of wholesale and retail shows that the Chabad Rebbes gave time to the single Jew, telling stories of the Ba'al HaTanya and the Rebbe Maharash. His answer: Chanukah brings the Shechinah down to those who cannot raise themselves, and the empty holders are hidden souls that must be lit, starting with one light, one individual. He closes with blessings.

en: 19 Kislev falls in the week of Chanukah, and the Mashgiach compares this to the week in which Tisha B'Av falls, which already carries some of that day's character.
Since a brachah does not rest on emptiness, the Mashgiach asks why the Chanukah brachah is made over a menorah most of whose holders are empty.
The Rebbes of Chabad enriched the Jewish people with Torah, emunah, warmth, deveikus and simcha, and every Jew is touched by Chabad's influence, directly or indirectly.
Beyond spreading Yiddishkeit to the many, the Chabad Rebbes gave themselves to the single Jew, knowing each individual is a whole world.
Chanukah is for those who cannot raise themselves: the Shechinah comes down below ten handbreadths to them.
The empty holders of the menorah are not empty: they are Jewish souls whose hidden spark must be kindled, so the brachah can rest on them.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Yud-Tes Kislev as a yom tov of light that leads into Chanukah. Rashi teaches that Hashem hid the first light for the tzaddikim, the Ba'al Shem Tov says it was hidden in the Torah, and the Bnei Yissaschar brings that the Chanukah lights hold this hidden light, the light of Moshiach. Chassidim, he says, must be like Chanukah lights and light up lost souls outside. Turning to the parsha, he brings the Midrash that while everyone was busy, Hashem was creating the light of Moshiach, and shows how Yehudah's descent and Tamar's sitting at 'the opening' bring that light into low places. Yehudah's admission and Tamar's waiting until the last moment show that Moshiach comes only through mesirus nefesh. He then speaks of Moshiach ben Yosef through Osnas, daughter of Dinah, and ends with the Chabad Rebbes, who lit up the outside with mesirus nefesh.

en: Yud-Tes Kislev is a yom tov of light that brings Jews into Chanukah, whose lights hold the hidden first light, the light of Moshiach.
Chassidim must be like Chanukah lights, lighting up lost souls in the public domain, the place where the forces of evil hold sway.
Everything in parshas Vayeishev, Yehudah's descent included, is part of Hashem's plan to create the light of Moshiach.
Moshiach can come only through mesirus nefesh, which the accusing forces cannot stand against; this is why Tamar waited until the last moment, so that Yehudah's mesirus nefesh would join hers.
The light of Moshiach must come in concealment, which is why Tamar was taken for a zonah.
Moshiach ben Yosef also appears in the parsha, through Osnas, daughter of Dinah and Shechem, who became Yosef's wife.
The Chabad Rebbes stood at the opening with mesirus nefesh and lit up the outside, rekindling souls that had fallen into the kelipos.

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Yehudah's great test, admitting 'she is more righteous than I' on the spot, with no time to weigh his shame. He explains that Tamar waited until the last moment because Moshiach comes only through mesirus nefesh, hers and Yehudah's together, and that his light must come in concealment, which is why she was taken for a zonah.

title.en: Moshiach ben Yosef and Osnas

summary.en: The Mashgiach turns to Moshiach ben Yosef, also found in the parsha. He brings Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer and Targum Yonasan that Osnas was the daughter of Dinah from Shechem, a kelipah that seized the soul of Moshiach ben Yosef, and explains why Dinah, who was once to have been Yosef, provides Yosef's match.

title.en: A shining lantern; the vengeance of Yosef

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Chabad as a flaming lantern around which all gather, rekindling souls fallen into the kelipos, with the power of the mitzvah of lighting the Chanukah light. He closes with Rashi on Pinchas avenging Yosef on Midian, and blesses all with a good week, a bright Chanukah and the light of Moshiach.

title.en: Another speaker

summary.en: Another speaker.

oneLiner.en: For Yud-Tes Kislev, the Mashgiach explains why the Alter Rebbe revealed Chassidus through a niggun: creation, Torah and above all Shabbos are built of seven 'voices' of song, and the seventh in every set is the one that sings.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the tradition that the Maggid of Mezritch revealed three things to the Alter Rebbe, the third being that he would reveal Chassidus through a niggun, and with the Alter Rebbe's early teaching on the Mishnah that 'all who have a song go out with song', which roused the scholars of Shklov until he answered their questions with a niggun. He brings the Tikkunei Zohar that a heavenly chamber of teshuvah opens only with song, which is why musical notes are called keys. The world was created with seven voices, the seven voices of Havu laHashem, one for each day and middah. In every set of seven the seventh is beloved and sings: Shabbos, Eretz Yisrael, the Kinneres, the zamer among the animals, and David among the ushpizin. Since the Torah is the blueprint of the world, it too is song, and so a niggun could answer questions in Torah. The talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov revealed what Shabbos is and poured their souls into its zemiros.

en: According to the Chabad tradition, the Maggid told the Alter Rebbe that his revelation of Chassidus would come through a niggun.
The world was created with seven voices, the seven voices of Havu laHashem, each corresponding to a day of creation and one of the seven middos.
In every set of seven the seventh is beloved and is the one that sings: Shabbos among the days, Eretz Yisrael among the lands, the Kinneres among the seas.
Shabbos completes the seven voices and is the kinor of creation, the day that itself sings Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos.
Since the Torah is the blueprint of the world and is itself song, a niggun can open the understanding of Torah, which is how the Alter Rebbe answered the scholars of Shklov.
The talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov revealed to the world what Shabbos is and brought great fervor into the zemiros of Shabbos.

title.en: The Maggid's three revelations and the niggun in Shklov

summary.en: After a short introduction by the host of the melave malka, the Mashgiach relates the tradition that the Maggid revealed three things to the Alter Rebbe, the third that Chassidus would be revealed through a niggun. He tells of the Alter Rebbe's teaching on 'kol baalei hashir' and how he answered the questions of the Shklov scholars by singing a niggun.

title.en: Notes are keys; the world's seven voices

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tikkunei Zohar that Klal Yisrael will leave golus with a niggun and that a chamber of teshuvah opens only with song, which is why musical notes are called keys. He explains that the world was created with seven voices, the seven voices of Havu laHashem, one for each day: chesed, gevurah, tiferes and onward.

title.en: The seventh sings: Shabbos as the kinor of creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rav Mordechai of Lechovitch's saying about a Jew who can sing Shabbos, and explains it with Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer: of seven days, lands and seas, the seventh is Shabbos, Eretz Yisrael and the Kinneres, and every seventh is beloved. Shabbos is the one day that itself sings, and like the seven-stringed kinor of the Beis HaMikdash it completes the seven voices of creation.

title.en: Eretz Yisrael and the singing Kinneres

summary.en: Eretz Yisrael is the kinor among the lands, and the Kinneres, named for the kinor, is the shliach tzibbur of the seas. The Mashgiach tells how the Stoliner Rebbe patted the Blozhover Rebbe on the shoulder, and uses it to explain the unique wording of the pasuk that the border 'touches the shoulder of the Kinneres'.

title.en: The zamer, David, and Kabbalas Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the same pattern in the ten kosher animals: three behemos against the first three sefiros and seven chayos against the middos, the seventh being the zamer that sings. Among the seven ushpizin the seventh is David, who completes the kinor, and Kabbalas Shabbos leads through the mizmorim of the week into Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos.

title.en: The Torah is song; the zemiros of Shabbos

summary.en: Since the Torah is the blueprint of the world and David called it zemiros, a niggun can open the understanding of Torah, which is how the Alter Rebbe answered Shklov. The Mashgiach speaks of the three tenu'os of the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Maggid and the Alter Rebbe, of how the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov revealed Shabbos and its zemiros, and of the Slonimer parable of the warm inn, and closes with a tefillah for the geulah.

catalogTitle: Nissan - A Time for the Renewal of Faith

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pesach, the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu and of Yetzias Mitzrayim, is the source of emunah, and that its matzah and its springtime newness let a Jew absorb that emunah and renew himself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the first of the Ten Commandments, which ties emunah to Yetzias Mitzrayim, and explains that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the root of emunah. At Yetzias Mitzrayim Hashem showed that He created the world: the ten utterances of creation, which no one saw, were revealed in the ten plagues, and the last plague, of the firstborn, matches the first utterance, Bereishis. Hashem therefore wants the story told to the children and also eaten, through matzah. The Mashgiach shows by gematria that bread holds the Divine Name three times, and matzah the Name with its filling three times. Matzah, baked fast, is above time and place, while chametz is bound to them; it is the food of emunah. Pesach and milah alone carry kareis because they bind a Jew to Avraham, his root. Nisan, the spring, is a new beginning and the month of chesed, and the Mashgiach calls on each person to renew himself with it.

en: Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the root of emunah, and therefore it is the Yom Tov of emunah.
At Yetzias Mitzrayim Hashem revealed, through the ten plagues, the ten utterances with which He created the world.
Hashem wants Yetzias Mitzrayim not only told to the children but eaten, so that through the matzah it becomes part of a person.
Matzah is above time and place, while chametz is bound to them, so matzah is the food of emunah.
Pesach and milah are the only positive mitzvos that carry kareis, because both bind a Jew to Avraham Avinu, his root.
Nisan, the spring, is a new beginning and the month of chesed, and a person must renew himself together with all of creation.

title.en: Pesach, Avraham Avinu and the ten plagues

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the first commandment ties emunah to Yetzias Mitzrayim, that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, and that the ten plagues revealed the ten utterances of creation, with the plague of the firstborn matching Bereishis.

title.en: Telling the children and eating the story

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Hashem wants Yetzias Mitzrayim passed down to every kind of child, and why He also wants it eaten: matzah baked and eaten with intent absorbs the story and makes emunah part of a person.

title.en: Lechem, matzah and the Divine Name

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the special standing of bread and the hidden powers Hashem placed in it, then shows by gematria that bread is three times the Name Havaya, while matzah is three times the Name with its filling, a higher bread.

title.en: Matzah above time and place

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that everything in this world exists in time and place, that chametz rises through time and takes up space, and that matzah, baked in haste, stays above both; it is the food of emunah, and the Haggadah is said over it so it absorbs the story.

title.en: Kareis, milah and the spring

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why only Pesach and milah among the positive mitzvos carry kareis, and answers that both bind a Jew to Avraham Avinu, his root. He then describes Pesach as the spring, a new beginning for the whole world.

title.en: Nisan, chesed and renewing oneself

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the dispute whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nisan, explains Nisan as the month of chesed, the right side, and Tishrei as din, and calls on each person to renew himself with the spring; he closes with the haftarah of the dry bones and a brachah for the Yom Tov.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef went down to Egypt as the shliach of Yaakov to prepare a protection for Jews in exile, and that the Ba'al Shem Tov, his talmidim and the Lubavitcher Rebbe's shluchim carry the same shlichus of bringing light into the darkest places.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Yaakov sending Yosef with the words 'and bring me back word', and the rule that a man's shliach is like himself: in his great test Yosef was strengthened by knowing he was Yaakov's shliach. His mission was to prepare a path so that Jews could hold firm in the exile of Egypt, and he completed it, answering 'Hashem has made me master over all Egypt'. Hashem later sent the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Maggid and the Ba'al HaTanya with a like mission. Yosef's test came in Egypt, the 'nakedness of the land', on the day the Mashgiach identifies as Nittel, the longest night, when one cannot learn Torah. Chanukah, the twenty-fifth, stands against it: the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael and mesiras nefesh. Today is a long Nittel, and the Lubavitcher Rebbe's shluchim light extinguished souls; the Mashgiach tells how the Rebbe made him a shliach too.

en: Yosef withstood his great test by remembering that he was the shliach of Yaakov, and a man's shliach is like himself.
Yosef's mission was to set up a protection in Egypt through his tests, so that the Jews who came after him could hold firm in exile.
Yosef's test took place on the day of the gentiles' festival, which the Mashgiach identifies as Nittel, the darkest night of the year.
Chanukah, the twenty-fifth, corresponds to the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael and is the light of kedushah set against the darkness of that night.
The mitzvah of the Chanukah light is especially dear because Chanukah came to Jews through mesiras nefesh, just as Avraham's milah was dear to him because it came with pain.
In the darkness before Moshiach the Lubavitcher Rebbe gave his shluchim the power of 'a man's shliach is like himself' to light extinguished souls in the farthest places.

title.en: Yosef as the shliach of Yaakov

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef withstood his test as Yaakov's shliach, and that his mission was to prepare a protection for Jews in the exile of Egypt. He reads Yosef's answer 'Hashem has made me master over all Egypt' as the completion of that mission, and compares it to the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Maggid and the Ba'al HaTanya.

title.en: Yosef's test on Nittel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the test of Yosef was shaped by place and time: Egypt, the 'nakedness of the land', whose place America takes today, and the gentiles' festival, which he identifies as Nittel. Since one cannot learn Torah then, Yosef was protected by yiras Shamayim and by knowing he had a shlichus.

title.en: Chanukah, the twenty-fifth, against Nittel

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Toldos Yaakov Yosef's calculation that the first night of Chanukah fell at the tekufah, and the Zohar on the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael, to show that Chanukah is the light of kedushah set against Nittel. He explains why the Chanukah light is especially dear, and reads 'ad koh' and Yosef's 'k'hayom hazeh' as pointing to the twenty-fifth.

title.en: The long Nittel and the Rebbe's shluchim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar's story of a tzaddik who learned on Nittel, and says that the time before Moshiach is one long Nittel. Against it the Lubavitcher Rebbe sent shluchim with the power of 'a man's shliach is like himself' to light extinguished souls, and Chabad fought with mesiras nefesh in Russia, few against many, like the Chashmona'im.

title.en: How the Rebbe made the Mashgiach a shliach

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the Rebbe's mesiras nefesh to bring a spark even into the simplest souls, and tells how, before one of his summers in Yerushalayim, when he meant only to sit and learn, the Rebbe gave him a dollar for tzedakah 'in addition to what you will have when you say drashos in Yerushalayim'.

title.en: The shlichus of Yud-Tes Kislev

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the Chanukah light, lit outside where the sitra achra rules, to the shlichus of strengthening Jews until Moshiach, completed like Yosef's 'Hashem has made me master over all Egypt'. He calls the shluchim the continuation of Yud-Tes Kislev and closes with a brachah for the light of the geulah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the last test of Avraham Avinu, seeing Hashem from afar and going on with simple emunah despite questions, is the test of our generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha, and that the Tanya is the sefer that answers all its questions.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the hidden love for Hashem inherited from the Avos, which comes out in a test of emunah. The generations form one full form from head to heel, and ours is the heel, ikvesa d'Meshicha. He asks what the test of the akeidah was, since many Jews gave their lives. Following the Zohar on 'vayar es hamakom merachok', he explains that Hashem seemed far, Avraham's levels were taken from him and he had questions, yet he went with simple emunah. By the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, this tenth test belongs to the last generation. He brings the seventy groans of a woman in labor, and ends with the Tanya, which holds the answer to every question, and a blessing for all Jews together.

en: Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem inherited from the Avos, which comes out when he faces a test of emunah, even when his emunah cannot be seen.
The generations form one full form from head to heel; the generations of the Exodus and Matan Torah were the head, and ours are the heel, ikvesa d'Meshicha.
The test of the akeidah was that Hashem seemed far from Avraham, his levels were taken from him and he had questions, and he still went with simple emunah.
By the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, the tenth test of Avraham is the test of the last generation, the generation of questions.
The Tanya, whose author writes that it answers the questions people used to bring him, is the sefer in which a Jew of this generation finds the answer to every question.

title.en: Hidden emunah and the generation of the heel

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the hidden love for Hashem that a Jew inherits from the Avos and that comes out in a test of emunah. He describes the generations of hester panim, and explains that the generations form one full form from head to heel, with ours as the heel.

title.en: What was the test of the akeidah?

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a nisayon raises a person higher, describes Avraham's first test at Ur Kasdim, and asks what made the last test harder, since many Jews gave their lives. He answers from the Zohar on 'vayar es hamakom merachok': Hashem seemed far from Avraham, and all the levels he had worked for his whole life were taken from him.

title.en: Questions on the promise, and simple emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham had questions against Hashem's promise of 'ki b'Yitzchak', yet pushed them out of his mind and went with simple emunah, like a Jew saying Shema with closed eyes. Rashi's simple answer was one even a child could give, but in a test the answer does not occur to a person; unlike a goy, who leaves his god over a question, Avraham set his questions aside.

title.en: Our generation's test: the last of Avraham's ten

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for the children, with the examples of the famine, Mitzrayim and Pharaoh, and concludes that the tenth test belongs to the generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha. He brings the gematria of 'vayar es hamakom merachok', the words 'eikev asher shamata b'koli', and the seventy groans of a woman in labor set against the seventy words of Lamnatzei'ach Ya'ancha.

title.en: The Tanya answers every question

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem sent the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Maggid and the Ba'al HaTanya as the means to pass through the exile with its questions. From the Tanya's introduction he shows that its author wrote it to answer the questions people used to bring him, and that whoever learns it is among those who know him. He closes with emunah as the merit of the redemption, a story of a blessing he gave the Rebbe, and a wish for all Jews together.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the bond between Parshas Vayeshev, Chanukah and Yud-Tes Kislev: the hidden light of Moshiach comes down to the lowest places and is revealed only through mesiras nefesh, as shown by Yehudah, Tamar, Yosef, the Chashmonaim and the Rebbeim of Chabad.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the story of the Mezritcher Maggid testing the young Shneur Zalman as a ba'al korei on the bond of each parsha to its week, and asks what ties Vayeshev to Yud-Tes Kislev. Chanukah, he explains from the Bnei Yissaschar and the Maharal, is the revealing of the hidden light, the light of Moshiach. It goes below ten tefachim into the public domain, to light up fallen souls that even Shabbos cannot reach, which is why the Mishnah's one Chanukah halacha is about a light placed in the street. In Vayeshev the soul of Moshiach is hidden: Yehudah goes down, and Tamar waits until she is taken out to be burned, because only mesiras nefesh overcomes the Satan's opposition. Yosef's mesiras nefesh, the Chashmonaim's, the Alter Rebbe's, the Tzemach Tzedek's and the Rebbe Rayatz's follow the same line, and Chabad's work with mesiras nefesh is the bond of Yud-Tes Kislev to Chanukah and Vayeshev.

en: Chanukah is the revealing of the hidden light, the light of Moshiach, which every Jew carries hidden within him.
Unlike the Shechinah, which does not descend below ten tefachim, the light of Chanukah goes down into the public domain to light up fallen and extinguished souls.
The Mishnah's one Chanukah halacha, about a light set out in the public domain, carries the whole intent of Chanukah.
The soul of Moshiach is hidden in Parshas Vayeshev, where Yehudah goes down and Peretz is born.
Bringing Moshiach requires mesiras nefesh, the one thing the Satan cannot oppose; Tamar, Yehudah and Yosef each showed it.
The Rebbeim of Chabad, from the Alter Rebbe through the Rebbe Rayatz, did their work with mesiras nefesh, and this is the bond of Yud-Tes Kislev to Chanukah and Vayeshev.
