title.en: Chanukah, the hidden light below ten tefachim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah is the revealing of the hidden light of Moshiach, which goes down below ten tefachim to light up fallen souls, even those that Shabbos cannot reach. He asks why the Mishnah barely mentions Chanukah, and answers that its one halacha, about a light in the public domain, holds the whole intent of Chanukah.

title.en: Yehudah goes down; Tamar's test

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the soul of Moshiach is hidden in Vayeshev, in the birth of Peretz, with a parable of a merchant who hid his money in a thief's bag. Yehudah went down below his level to kindle the light of Moshiach. He asks why Tamar waited until she was taken out to be burned, putting Yehudah to a fearful test before the beis din.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh defeats the Satan

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that Tamar knew she was to bring Moshiach, and that twice before, through Er and Onan, the Satan had blocked it. Their souls came back as Peretz and Zerach. She saw that only mesiras nefesh is beyond the Satan's power, so she brought both herself and Yehudah to it.

title.en: Yosef, the Chashmonaim and the two Moshiachs

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Yosef, the root of Moshiach ben Yosef, who showed mesiras nefesh with Potiphar's wife and went down to Egypt. Both Moshiachs had to descend to the lowest place. Chanukah, the hidden light, came through the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh, and a Jew who lights the Chanukah lights kindles the light of Moshiach.

title.en: The Alter Rebbe and the Tzemach Tzedek

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the first chassidic sefer was called the Torah of Moshiach and roused accusation above, all the more when the Alter Rebbe spread the inner Torah more deeply, leading to his arrest. He did not deny being a talmid of the Ba'al Shem Tov, and he sent money to Eretz Yisrael with mesiras nefesh. Then he tells how the Tzemach Tzedek refused to sign a blank letter in Moscow.

title.en: The Rebbe Rayatz and the bond of Yud-Tes Kislev

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Rebbe Rayatz's mesiras nefesh in spreading Torah under the Communists and his demand that his Chassidim have it too. He concludes that this is the bond of Yud-Tes Kislev to Chanukah and Vayeshev: Chabad sends its people with mesiras nefesh to light up extinguished souls, and he closes with a brachah for the coming of Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that our emunah rests on a mesorah from Yetzias Mitzrayim and Sinai that Pesach is meant to pass down, and that complete emunah means seeing Hashem's hashgachah pratis in every detail, never saying 'if only'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that in the low generation before Moshiach, those raised in Torah homes carry the responsibility of passing emunah on. Our faith rests on what millions of Jews saw from Yetzias Mitzrayim to Matan Torah, written in the Torah while they were alive and handed down unchanged. Small differences between communities reflect the twelve shevatim, each with its own color, gate and path, while the Torah and Chazal's decrees bind everyone; disputes such as an eruv belong to the rabbanim, and the Chasam Sofer warns that machlokes can delay Moshiach. Pesach, the yom tov of emunah, exists to pass this down, which is why it carries kareis. Habakkuk based everything on emunah, so one must learn it, not treat it as a habit. A story of neshamos protesting endless gilgulim ends with Hashem asking only for emunah without 'would have'. The Mashgiach illustrates hashgachah pratis and calls Pesach a time to strengthen emunah.

en: Jewish emunah rests on a mesorah no other faith has: millions saw Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah, it was written down while they were alive, and the same Sefer Torah is found wherever Jews are.
Differences in minhagim and small details between communities stem from the twelve shevatim, each with its own color, gate and path, while all of Klal Yisrael shares the Torah and Chazal's decrees.
Pesach exists to pass emunah from generation to generation, which is why it alone among the yomim tovim carries kareis.
Emunah must be learned and researched, not lived as an inherited habit, since it is the Jew's very neshamah for which whole communities gave their lives.
Complete emunah means believing that every detail is directed by Hashem, so a person never says 'would have, could have, should have'.

title.en: Our responsibility and the mesorah from Sinai

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that in the low generation before Moshiach, those raised in Torah homes must strengthen themselves against a new, high-tech yetzer hara and pass emunah down. He describes the unparalleled mesorah: millions saw Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah, and the Sefer Torah written then is the same wherever Jews live.

title.en: Twelve shevatim, twelve colors, twelve gates

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that small differences in Sifrei Torah and minhagim come from the twelve shevatim, each with its own gate in heaven, stone on the choshen and flag color. He brings Rashi on the flags, a reading of 'shoftim v'shotrim' with 'lishvatecha', the gates at the end of Yechezkel, the Zohar on twelve gates for tefillah, and the twelve paths at Kriyas Yam Suf.

title.en: Machlokes, the Chasam Sofer, and what binds all

summary.en: Applying this to a dispute over an eruv, the Mashgiach cites the Chazon Ish that each person follows his rav, and the Chasam Sofer that machlokes in the generation of great Acharonim held back Moshiach. He stresses that differences are only in small details, while the Torah and Chazal's decrees bind every Jew, and this unbroken mesorah is our strength against apikorsim.

title.en: Pesach, the yom tov of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mitzvah of emunah is 'Anochi Hashem Elokecha asher hotzeisicha', since the ten makkos revealed the ten maamaros of creation, and that Pesach is the yom tov for passing emunah to the children, which is why it carries kareis. Before Moshiach the yetzer hara fights hardest, so, as the Gemara says Habakkuk based all on emunah, one must learn and research emunah rather than treat it as a tradition.

title.en: The neshamos who protested their gilgulim

summary.en: After describing communities that gave their lives rather than give up emunah, the Mashgiach tells of a tzaddik who, after Kiddush Levanah, told his talmidim what he had seen: neshamos tired of being sent down again and again went from malach to malach up to Hashem, asking what He wants of them. Hashem answers that they should go down and have emunah.

title.en: Hashgachah pratis: no 'would have'

summary.en: Hashem's condition is emunah so complete that a person never says 'would have', illustrated by a man who blames his wife for a missed train and a lost deal. The Mashgiach describes hashgachah pratis down to a falling straw and the kernels in a loaf of bread, Hashem as the One who cares for a person more than anyone, and closes that Pesach is a time for introspection and fortifying emunah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that Chanukah, the last of the mitzvos, is the mitzvah of mesiras nefesh for the holiness and separateness of Klal Yisrael, like Yaakov's sons at Shechem, and that the Chassidim of Chabad are the Chashmonaim of today.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the 620 mitzvos, the 613 and the seven of the Rabbanan, which match the 620 letters of the Aseres Hadibros, and with the 600,000 letters of the Torah that match the 600,000 souls of Israel. The last letters stand for the lowest souls of the generation before Moshiach, and the last mitzvah, ner Chanukah, stands for the last Jew. The Chashmonaim went to war with mesiras nefesh, and Chabad brought the same mesiras nefesh to Russia; he sees them as today's Chashmonaim. He then asks why Yaakov received the name Yisrael only after Shechem, and explains that the people of Shechem wanted to swallow up Yaakov's family, while the brothers, saying 'we will be one people', were really pleading with Hashem. Through Shabbos, techum and ner Chanukah he shows that Klal Yisrael must stay within the reshus hayachid of Hashem. He closes with the Chabad shluchim in Mumbai and a brachah.

en: Every Jew is rooted in one of the 600,000 letters of the Torah, and the last letters are the lowest souls of the generation before Moshiach.
Ner Chanukah, the last of the seven mitzvos of the Rabbanan, corresponds to the lowest Jew, the last one in Klal Yisrael.
The Chashmonaim went against the mighty Greek empire with mesiras nefesh, not to die but to win, and the Chassidim of Chabad are the Chashmonaim of today.
Yaakov earned the name Yisrael only after the mesiras nefesh at Shechem, which was a war for the holiness of the Jewish family, like the war of Chanukah.
Klal Yisrael must stay within the reshus hayachid of Hashem; mixing with the nations is like carrying out from the private domain into the public domain.

title.en: The last letter and the last mitzvah

summary.en: After a sponsorship notice, the Mashgiach explains that the 620 mitzvos match the letters of the Aseres Hadibros and that every Jew is rooted in a letter of the Torah. The last letters are the lowest souls before Moshiach, and the last mitzvah, ner Chanukah, stands for the last Jew.

title.en: The Chashmonaim and Chabad: mesiras nefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the tefillah of the Bnei Yissaschar before lighting, asking to merit the mesiras nefesh of the Chashmonaim, who fought to win. He describes how the Rebbes of Chabad brought mesiras nefesh to Russia, and gives a remez that 19 Kislev is the gematria of Chashmonaim.

title.en: The name Yisrael and the war of Shechem

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Hashem waited until after Shechem to give Yaakov the name Yisrael. He brings the Divrei Yoel that the people of Shechem accepted milah to stop a separate Jewish people from arising, and the seforim that the war of Shechem parallels the war of the Chashmonaim.

title.en: Shema Yisrael, and a tzaddik's glass of milk

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that the 24 days before Chanukah match the letters of Baruch Shem and the 25th day matches the 25 letters of Shema Yisrael, the words of mesiras nefesh. He explains that tzaddikim speak to Hashem even while speaking to people, and tells the story of Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz and the glass of milk.

title.en: A wall around Klal Yisrael: techum and reshus hayachid

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when the brothers said 'we will be one people' they were pleading with Hashem, and that Yaakov set up techumin at Shechem. Through the Zohar on Shabbos as reshus hayachid and carrying out as leaving Hashem's domain, and the ner Chanukah placed at the door to the public domain, he shows that Klal Yisrael must keep a boundary between itself and the nations.

title.en: The name Yisrael earned; the shluchim of today

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that the name Yisrael came only after the mesiras nefesh of Shechem. He describes the Chabad shluchim who went on after the killing of the shluchim in Mumbai, calls them the Chanukah of the generation, and closes with a brachah.

oneLiner.en: Through the Midrash of the simple Jew who taught that the nations will return Yaakov's gifts, the Mashgiach explains that Jewish souls cut off from their root will be brought back, and that this is the work of the Baal HaTanya and his chassidim in kindling lost souls.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash in which a simple Jew, an am ha'aretz, asks Rabbi Yehoshua to repeat his teaching in his name: the passuk 'minchah yashivu' means that in the days of Moshiach the nations will return the gifts Yaakov sent Esav. Why did he want it said in his name? The Mashgiach answers with the Maharal on the Mishnah that one who says a thing in the name of its speaker brings geulah: returning a word to its root brings Jews back to their root. He explains that Yaakov's sheep were Jewish souls, that at the struggle with Esav's angel later generations fell under Esav's power, and that this am ha'aretz, rooted in those souls, sensed it and sought their redemption. He connects this to the unlit lamps of the Chanukah menorah, to the Baal HaTanya's work of kindling extinguished souls, to a story of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, and to 19 Kislev as the sounding of the great shofar.

en: The am ha'aretz in the Midrash taught that 'minchah yashivu' means the nations will return to Moshiach the gifts Yaakov sent Esav.
Following the Maharal, one who says a thing in the name of its speaker returns the word to its root, and in that merit the Jews, cut off in galus, return to their root.
Yaakov's sheep were Jewish souls that he redeemed from Lavan, and they became the six hundred thousand who left Mitzrayim and received the Torah.
When Esav's angel touched Yaakov's thigh, he gained a hold over Jews of later generations who lack the power of Torah against the yetzer hara.
The unlit lamps of the Chanukah menorah are part of the menorah and wait to be kindled, as lost Jewish souls wait to be brought back.
The work the Baal HaTanya instilled in his chassidim and in the Rebbes after him is to kindle extinguished Jewish souls with mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The am ha'aretz's teaching on 'minchah yashivu'

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks pardon for not standing before the Baal HaTanya, then brings the Midrash in which an am ha'aretz asks Rabbi Yehoshua to say his teaching in his name: the nations will return Yaakov's gifts to Moshiach. He asks why the man wanted it said in his name, and how he merited that it is learned every Vayishlach.

title.en: Saying a word in its speaker's name brings geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal on the Mishnah that saying a thing in its speaker's name brings geulah: it returns the word to its root, and so returns the Jews to theirs. He explains that each Jew has a letter in the Torah, and that the angel who touched Yaakov's thigh gained power over later Jews who lack Torah, the only spice against the yetzer hara.

title.en: Yaakov's flocks were Jewish souls

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yaakov grieved over giving away animals when he had so many, and answers that they were Jewish souls he had redeemed from Lavan. Because the struggle with Esav's angel had already given Esav a hold over later generations, he had to hand them over; the am ha'aretz, rooted in those souls, made his chiddush that they will return.

title.en: A personal geulah and the unlit Chanukah lamps

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the am ha'aretz sensed his own root and sought a geulah for himself and those like him, and that this is why every Vayishlach the Midrash brings them closer. He brings the Tanya on birur nitzotzos in the time before Moshiach, and explains why one lights in a menorah of eight lamps though some stay unlit.

title.en: Kindling extinguished souls: the Stuttgart matzos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the work of the Baal HaTanya, his chassidim and the Rebbes after him is to kindle extinguished Jewish souls with mesiras nefesh. He tells a story from the Lubavitch seforim of a package of matzos the Lubavitcher Rebbe sent to the first Jew in Stuttgart, who was about to leave Yiddishkeit.

title.en: 19 Kislev and the great shofar

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the thousands of shluchim who kindle souls everywhere as an awakening of the days of Moshiach. He recalls a farbrengen of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, before he was Rebbe, where he gave a gematria linking 19 Kislev to the great shofar, and closes with the call to return to the root and kindle Jewish souls.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the year after shemittah, the year of Hakhel, can become the 'eighth', the year of Moshiach, and that this is why the children are brought to Hakhel: they will sing the shirah when Moshiach is revealed.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the new ways of the Lubavitcher Rebbe concerning children: before the Yom Kippur War he called again and again for children to say Tehillim, daven and learn, based on 'from the mouths of babes', and he brought children to hear the Aseres Hadibros. Another such chiddush was the year of Hakhel, which he made a matter of the whole year. The Mashgiach then asks why the Torah commands bringing the little ones to Hakhel, when the Gemara says it is only to reward those who bring them. He explains that after the seven years of the shemittah cycle comes either a new cycle or an 'eighth', which is Moshiach, as the Gemara says that Moshiach comes on motzaei shviis. With this he explains when we say Magen David, the king's reading at Hakhel, and why we wait for Moshiach. He concludes that at a Hakhel of Moshiach the children will sing shirah as at the Yam Suf, so they must be brought.

en: The Lubavitcher Rebbe introduced new ways of involving children, calling on them to say Tehillim, daven and learn before the Yom Kippur War, based on 'from the mouths of babes'.
After the seventh year of shemittah, the next year can either begin a new cycle or be the 'eighth', and the eighth means Moshiach; this is why the Gemara says Moshiach comes on motzaei shviis.
Maftir is the eighth aliyah, the aliyah of Moshiach, and that is why its brachah may say Magen David although Shemoneh Esrei says only Magen Avraham.
Sukkos of the year after shemittah, the time of Hakhel, can be a Yom Tov of Moshiach, when the soul of Moshiach could join the king reading the Torah.
The children are brought to Hakhel so that, if it turns out to be the Hakhel of Moshiach, they will be there to sing the shirah, as the infants did at the Yam Suf.

title.en: The Rebbe's chiddushim with children

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Lubavitcher Rebbe as a soul of renewal, whose great chiddush was his devotion to children. He recalls how, weeks before the Yom Kippur War, the Rebbe repeatedly called for children to say Tehillim, daven and learn, and how he brought children to the Aseres Hadibros.

title.en: The year of Hakhel and the little ones

summary.en: The Mashgiach says this year is a year of Hakhel, which the Rebbe made a matter of the whole year, with special attention to the children. He brings the Gemara that the little ones come to Hakhel only to give reward to those who bring them, and calls this a difficult answer.

title.en: Motzaei shviis: the eighth year

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that seven is nature and eight is above nature. After the seventh year either a new cycle begins or the 'eighth' comes, which is Moshiach, as the Gemara says Moshiach comes on motzaei shviis; he shows the same with Yovel and with motzaei Shabbos.

title.en: Magen David and the eighth aliyah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that David asked that a brachah end with his name as with Avraham's, and was refused, against a Midrash that David is greater than the Avos. He answers that both are true, and that this is revealed at maftir, the eighth aliyah, where the brachah does say Magen David.

title.en: Hakhel as a Yom Tov of Moshiach; why we wait

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Sukkos after shemittah has two meanings, and Hakhel is a Yom Tov of Moshiach: when the king reads, the soul of Moshiach could join him. He then brings the Gemara that Hashem too waits, and that we wait in order to receive reward; the waiting itself brings Moshiach.

title.en: The children's shirah and the hilula

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that infants at the Yam Suf saw the Shechinah and sang 'zeh Keili', and says that at a Hakhel of Moshiach the children will surely sing; this is why they are brought. He ties this to the reward of waiting, and closes with the hilula of the Ba'al HaTanya and the Maggid, wishing that Moshiach be revealed this year.

catalogTitle: The Disintegration of Society at the Time of עקביתא דמשיחא

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows how the signs of the generation before Moshiach listed in the Gemara in Sotah are visible today, and explains that a Jew placed in this generation is meant to withstand its tests by keeping good company and holding on to emunah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the power of a person's company: the Rambam tells one to leave a bad neighborhood, the Chazon Ish told the Satmar Rav to run to the yeshiva, and a chassid was saved from sin only by shame before his friends. The Gemara's zarzir, a bird that keeps company with the raven, belongs to its kind. Today, he says, the outside world enters a Jew's own home, and souls are sent into this generation precisely to withstand these tests, as Yosef did in Mitzrayim. He then explains why the signs of Ikvesa d'Meshicha appear on the 49th daf of Sotah, matching the 49 days of the Omer and the lowest level before redemption. Going through the Braisa, he shows its signs today: chutzpah, rising prices, a government turned to atheism, immoral universities, poverty of those from Eretz Yisrael, rebellious children and leaders who follow their congregations. Still, he concludes, one can rely on Hashem and remain a faithful Jew.

en: Company is the strongest influence on a person: what fear of Gehinnom and even a Rebbe cannot do, friends can do.
Unlike earlier generations, which lived apart from the nations, today the outside world enters the Jewish home through media and permissiveness.
Each soul is placed by Heaven into its generation for its tests and its tikkun; this generation was sent down to withstand these trials.
The signs of Ikvesa d'Meshicha appear on daf 49 of Sotah, corresponding to the 49th, lowest day of the Omer count before the giving of the Torah.
The signs of the Braisa, such as chutzpah, rising prices, a government turned to atheism and rebellion of children, are visible in today's society.
Even in the last moments before redemption, one can rely on Hashem and remain a faithful Jew.

title.en: Sotah, the Omer and the 49th level

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the sotah brings a barley offering, as does the Omer on the second day of Pesach, and that the 49 days of counting lead from the highest to the lowest level before the Torah is given. Since Masechta Sotah has 49 dapim, the Braisa of Ikvesa d'Meshicha on its 49th daf speaks of the last, lowest stage before the redemption.

title.en: Chutzpah and rising prices

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the Braisa's first signs: chutzpah at its peak, seen in the loss of respect for teachers, in protected subversive parades and in laws that permit wrongdoing, and prices rising even where supply is plentiful.

title.en: Government turned to atheism; schools of immorality

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that governments were always religious, even forcing their faith on Jews, while today the state is atheist; he tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov left a wagon whose driver did not cross himself. He then reads the 'house of meeting' as the institution of higher learning, now mixed and the source of immorality.

title.en: Poverty, rebellious children and failing leaders

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes people from Eretz Yisrael wandering abroad to collect money to marry off children, the young no longer standing for the old, children rebelling against parents, and leaders who, like a dog looking back at its master, follow their congregations. He concludes that even in these last moments one can rely on Hashem and remain a faithful Jew.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the name Yisrael is the havdalah between Jew and gentile, which Yaakov fought for with the angel before Shechem, which the Greeks tried to erase, and for which the Lubavitcher Rebbe fought in the battle over 'who is a Jew'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Yaakov, who in this week's parsha insists that the angel concede the blessings and confirm his name now, not later at Beis El. He links this to the Lubavitcher Rebbe's battle over 'who is a Jew', and calls it an old battle: the war of Yaakov's sons with Shechem. Citing Tzidkas Hatzaddik, he explains that a Jew is one who calls himself Yisrael. Shechem wanted to merge with the Jews, and the Greeks decreed against Chodesh, Shabbos and milah because these are the havdalah between Israel and the nations. Yaakov needed the name Yisrael fixed before reaching Shechem, the place of Yosef, of kedushas habris and of priah. That is why Yosef was sent there, and why Yaakov set techumin there. Chanukah is the victory of that havdalah, and its joy is the joy of being a Jew called Yisrael.

en: According to Tzidkas Hatzaddik, a Jew is one who calls himself by the name Yisrael; one who does not call himself a Jew is outside the name.
Chodesh, Shabbos and milah, which the Greeks decreed against, are the mitzvos that separate Israel from the nations.
Yaakov insisted that the angel confirm the name Yisrael before he reached Shechem, because Shechem would be a war against that separation.
Shechem is the place of Yosef and of kedushas habris, specifically of priah, the completion of milah.
Chanukah is the victory of the havdalah between Israel and the nations and the honor of the name Yisrael.
The joy of Chanukah is a Jew's joy in being a Jew and being called Yisrael.

title.en: Why Yaakov needed the name Yisrael before Shechem

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the klipah of Yavan set out to cancel the havdalah, as Shechem had tried before. Yaakov knew a war awaited him in Shechem, so he needed his name fixed as Yisrael, the name of a people set apart; the angel wept because he understood he would lose. Shechem became Yosef's portion.

title.en: Priah, Yosef and Shechem

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that milah alone does not fully separate a Jew, since the sons of Keturah also circumcise; priah does, and it comes from Yosef. He asks why Yosef had to be sent to Shechem first, and answers that Shechem is the place of kedushas habris and of priah, where Yosef drew strength for his trials in Mitzrayim.

title.en: Techumin in Shechem and the light of Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yaakov set techumin in Shechem because techumin too are a separation, and that 'bein kodesh lechol' equals 'mekom Shechem' in gematria. Chanukah is the victory of the havdalah and the honor of the name Yisrael, and the Lubavitcher Rebbe fought for it when others were indifferent.

title.en: The joy of being called Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the name Yisrael is a praise of the Jews and also of Hashem, Who is called Elokei Yisrael. He brings the haskamah to the Tanya and a Lubavitch tradition that 'Yisrael' there means the Ba'al Shem Tov, and concludes with the Rambam that the days of Chanukah are days of joy: the joy of being a Jew.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that Chanukah, the ninth, hidden 'tes', reveals the hidden light (or haganuz) in every Jew, even the lowest, and that this is the heart of Tanya chapter 32: to love every Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Tanya chapter 32: even the lowest Jew carries a hidden spark of good, so one must love him and draw him close. He tells the Chiddushei HaRim's story of the Rebbe of Lublin, who saw on an informer's kvitel that the man lit up all the worlds, because he had written it while lighting Chanukah candles, which kindle the hidden light in every Jew. He then asks why Yosef's second dream is called 'chalom acher'. Two foundations follow: kedushah is built on ten while the power that fights the sitra achra needs eleven; and, from the Mei HaShiloach, the ninth pasuk of every sedra holds a hidden secret, like the letter tes and Yosef, the ninth. The ninth pasuk of Vayeshev is Yosef's second dream, a Chanukah dream, whose gematria Yaakov hinted at. Chanukah brings the Shechinah down to the lowest Jews. He closes with loving Hashem and loving every Jew in all circumstances.

en: Following Tanya chapter 32, the Mashgiach teaches that even the lowest Jew has hidden good in him, so one hates only the evil in him and loves him and draws him close.
Chanukah lights kindle the or haganuz, the hidden light, in every Jew, which is why the Rebbe of Lublin saw an informer lighting up all the worlds while he lit Chanukah candles.
The ninth pasuk of each sedra holds a hidden secret, like the letter tes whose good is hidden inside it and like Yosef, the hidden ninth sefirah.
Yosef's second dream, the ninth pasuk of Vayeshev, is 'a different dream': a dream of Chanukah and of the hidden light.
Chanukah is the one exception to the rule that the Shechinah never comes below ten tefachim: it comes down to weekday Jews, to the lowest, to awaken them.
The Mashgiach closes that just as one must love Hashem in all circumstances, one must love a fellow Jew in all circumstances, hating his deeds but loving him for his soul.

title.en: Chalom acher, and the power of eleven

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yosef's second dream is called 'chalom acher' and not a repeated dream, and why it took twenty-two years to come true. As a first foundation he explains that kedushah is built on ten, while the power that fights the sitra achra must have eleven, as in the eleven spices of the ketores, the eleven goat-hair curtains and 'eleven days from Chorev'.

title.en: The hidden ninth pasuk and the letter tes

summary.en: As a second foundation the Mashgiach brings the Mei HaShiloach on Balak: the ninth pasuk of every sedra holds a hidden secret, alluding to Yosef, the ninth and hidden one. He adds the Zohar that the good of the letter tes is hidden inside it, and the Bnei Yissaschar that the or haganuz is hidden in the Chanukah lights.

title.en: Yosef's dream of Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the ninth pasuk of Vayeshev is Yosef's second dream, a dream of Chanukah. Chanukah is the one exception to the rule that the Shechinah never descends below ten, coming down to weekday Jews; Yosef, a hidden soul, is the soul of Chanukah, and the Shelah says Yosef equals 'Melech Yavan' in gematria. He also speaks of the eleven stars that fight the sitra achra.

title.en: Yaakov's wonder: 'mah hachalom hazeh'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Yaakov's 'mah hachalom hazeh' as an exclamation of wonder, like 'mah ahavti sorasecha': Yaakov understood that Yosef had dreamt of Chanukah, and 'hachalom' equals Chanukah in gematria. It is revealed in the ninth month, the ninth sedra and the ninth pasuk, and the Gemara says that one who sees a tes in his dream has a good sign.

title.en: Thirty-six lights; the King goes to the tannery

summary.en: From the Bnei Yissaschar the Mashgiach brings that the first tes in the Torah, 'ki tov', is the or haganuz, and four times tes is thirty-six, the number of Chanukah lights. Chanukah, a weekday yom tov, takes the Shechinah out of the bounds of kedushah to where a Jew is, like the Zohar's parable of the King who goes to his queen in the tannery; Purim likewise brings the kedushah outside the wall.

title.en: Loving Hashem and loving every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Tanya chapter 32 the heart of the Tanya, the avodah of all the Lubavitcher Rebbes. He closes with the two pesukim of 've'ahavta': as one loves Hashem in all circumstances, knowing all is for good, so one loves a Jew in all circumstances, and he wishes a good week and a bright Chanukah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Jewish people are Hashem's terumah, which can never be redeemed or exchanged, because every Jew holds an inner point of 'I want' that sin cannot reach, and from this he teaches that one must love and draw close every Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that a non-kohen may fulfill the mitzvah of esrog with an esrog of terumah, and with Rashi's remark that terumah has no redemption; Rashi calls one who says it can be redeemed a rasha. Why such sharpness over a differing view? He brings a Midrash of a king who sent away his queen yet ordered jewelry for her, and the passuk calling Yisroel Hashem's 'first of His crop', which is terumah. Through the Ramban on the forty lashes, of which only thirty-nine are given, and the Rambam on 'I want', he shows that every Jew has a point that sin cannot touch, revealed on Yom Kippur, whose gematria equals 'I want'. Saying Jews can be exchanged is Bilaam's view. Tanya chapter 32 and the passuk of helping one's enemy's donkey teach that one must love the good in every Jew and draw him close, as Chabad houses do.

en: The Jewish people are called Hashem's 'first of His crop', which is terumah, and just as terumah can never be redeemed, Jews can never stop being Hashem's.
Every Jew has an inner point where he does not sin, and this is why the Torah's forty lashes are reduced to thirty-nine.
That point is the 'I want' of the Rambam and the 'part of G-d above' of the Tanya, and it is revealed on Yom Kippur, the fortieth day of teshuvah.
Rashi calls one who says terumah can be redeemed a rasha because that is Bilaam's view, that Yisroel can be exchanged for another nation.
One must love and draw close every Jew, even a rasha, because he has a part of G-d above, and this is the point of Chabad and its Rebbes.
Even where one may hate a sinner, one must love the good part in him, and compassion nullifies hatred.

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara on an esrog of terumah and Rashi's words that terumah has no redemption, and asks why Rashi calls one who says otherwise a rasha. He brings a Midrash of a king and his queen, and the passuk that calls Yisroel Hashem's terumah.

title.en: The point of 'I want' in every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Ramban on the forty lashes, of which only thirty-nine are given, through the Rambam's 'I want' and the Tanya: every Jew has a point where sin does not reach. That point is revealed on Yom Kippur, whose gematria equals 'I want'.

title.en: Bilaam's view and the heart of Tanya

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers his opening question: saying terumah can be redeemed is Bilaam's view, that Jews can be exchanged for another nation. From Tanya chapter 32 he teaches that one must love and draw close every Jew, as Chabad houses and Lubavitcher chassidim do, and that Hashem refused to listen to Bilaam because He loves Yisroel.

title.en: Loving the good in the one you may hate

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how the Torah can speak of a Jew one hates, and explains with Chazal, the Tanya and Targum Onkelos that one may hate the bad in a sinner but must love the good in him and help him come close. He closes with a blessing in the merit of the Baal Hilula that all Jewish hearts be drawn close to their Father in Heaven.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that after Pesach, the Yom Tov of emunah, the Torah warns against the two things that damage emunah most, forbidden food and breaches of kedushah, and describes how the Satan in our generation floods the world with both.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by recalling that Pesach is the Yom Tov of emunah and that matzah, which the Zohar calls the food of emunah, makes emunah part of a Jew's body. The two sedras read right after Pesach, Shemini on forbidden foods and Acharei on arayos, deal with the two greatest damagers of emunah. Treif food clogs the heart, as the Gemara reads 'venitmeisem' as 'venitamtem', and takes away a person's taste in Yiddishkeit and Shabbos. In the days before Moshiach the Satan, fighting for his life, floods the market with treif and doubtful hechsherim. The Mashgiach tells of the Skverer Rebbe's extreme care, the Rambam's answer to doubters of techiyas hameisim, and a tzaddik who found a kernel of wheat in his Pesach soup because he had not davened. He then turns to kedushas habris, describes the streets and media of today, and urges escaping the city, guarding the home, and keeping good company.

en: Pesach is the Yom Tov of emunah, and by eating matzah, the food of emunah, a Jew internalizes emunah into his very body.
The sedras after Pesach, Shemini and Acharei, address forbidden food and arayos because these two damage emunah more than anything else.
Forbidden food clogs the heart, so that a person loses his feeling and taste in Yiddishkeit and in Shabbos.
In the days before Moshiach the Satan, fighting for his life, floods the market with treif and unreliable hechsherim.
Care in kashrus is not enough on its own; a person must also daven to Hashem not to stumble.
The Satan of this generation has concentrated on breaching kedushah through the streets and the media, a test no earlier generation faced.

title.en: Matzah, the food of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that Pesach is the Yom Tov of emunah and that eating matzah makes emunah part of a Jew's body. He then notes that the sedras after Pesach, Shemini and Acharei, deal with forbidden food and arayos, the two greatest damagers of emunah.

title.en: Treif food dulls the taste of Yiddishkeit

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Jews who taste the sweetness of Shabbos with bochurim who complain they feel nothing on Shabbos, and says they probably ate treif. He brings the Gemara that reads 'venitmeisem' as 'venitamtem': forbidden food clogs the heart.

title.en: The Satan floods the market with treif

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the days before Moshiach the Satan, sensing danger, fights with extra strength and floods the market with forbidden food. Before World War I no Jew ate treif; today ingredients are so complex and hechsherim so unreliable that hardly anyone can say he never ate treif.

title.en: The Skverer Rebbe and the Rambam's letter

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Skverer Rebbe refused freshly squeezed orange juice because his father never drank it, and baked his bread all year from wheat he had cut himself. He then brings the Rambam's letter answering people who doubted techiyas hameisim: they ask because they ate forbidden food.

title.en: Care and tefillah: the kernel in the soup

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges care in kashrus together with tefillah not to stumble, and tells of a tzaddik who cleaned for a month yet found a kernel of wheat in his soup at the Seder. Through a dream question he learned it happened because he had not davened for a kosher Pesach, and how a bird dropped it down the chimney.

title.en: Kedushas habris and the streets of today

summary.en: Turning to the second damager, the Mashgiach links Pesach and bris milah to Avraham Avinu, the root of emunah, and explains that bris milah is a lifelong mitzvah of guarding kedushah. He describes how today's streets, laws and media have made this test greater than in any generation, bringing the Medrash on 'goy naval' in Haazinu.

title.en: Practical guarding: city, home and friends

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up that emunah is ruined by forbidden food and breaches of kedushas habris, and urges whoever can to leave the city in summer and to keep radio, television and inciting literature out of the home. He stresses the influence of friends and brings the Rambam that one must move away from a bad neighborhood.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the animals Yaakov sent to Esav were Jewish souls under Esav's sway, which Esav will return to Moshiach, and that the Rebbes of Lubavitch and their Chabad houses have already begun this return.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the teaching of the seforim that Yaakov's sheep were Jewish souls held captive in Lavan's house, and that his twenty years there were spent redeeming them. He asks how Yaakov could then hand some of them to Esav, and answers with a Midrash: Yaakov did not choose, and the animals that came on their own were those connected to Esav. Another Midrash, said by an am ha'aretz to Rabbi Hoshaya, reads 'minchah yashivu': the nations will return the gift to Moshiach. Why an am ha'aretz? The wrestling with Esav's angel was a prelude to the meeting with Esav, and the angel touched the gid hanasheh, the part of Yaakov that holds the souls of Jews far from Torah. By gematria the passuk of the gift equals 'es gid hanasheh', and the 580 animals equal Se'ir. The am ha'aretz, rooted in that passuk, sensed his own return. The Mashgiach concludes that the Rebbes of Lubavitch and their shluchim have begun this return, a foretaste of Moshiach.

en: Yaakov's twenty years with Lavan were spent redeeming his sheep, which were Jewish souls held captive by the sitra achra.
The animals Yaakov sent to Esav were souls under Esav's jurisdiction: Jews who do not learn Torah and have not accepted the yoke of Heaven.
The Midrash reads 'minchah yashivu' to mean that Esav will give the animals back when Moshiach comes.
Every soul has its root in a passuk of the Torah.
The return of these souls has already begun through the Rebbes of Lubavitch and the Chabad houses in nearly every town.

title.en: Yaakov's sheep were Jewish souls

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the teaching of the seforim that Yaakov's sheep were Jewish souls captive in Lavan's house, which Yaakov redeemed during his twenty years there and brought to Eretz Yisrael. He adds that the Ohev Yisrael remembered being one of Yaakov's sheep and even the niggun Yaakov played for them.

title.en: Minchah yashivu and the wrestling as prelude

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how Yaakov could give his redeemed animals to Esav, and brings the Midrash that the animals chose themselves, and the Midrash of the am ha'aretz who taught Rabbi Hoshaya that 'minchah yashivu' means the gift will be returned to Moshiach. He asks why an am ha'aretz revealed this, and begins by explaining that Yaakov's wrestling with Esav's angel was a prelude to his meeting with Esav.

title.en: The souls of the gid hanasheh

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that all Jewish souls were part of Yaakov, and that the souls of the gid hanasheh, which Esav's angel touched, are the amei ha'aretz under Esav's sway; these went to Esav as the gift. He gives a gematria linking the passuk of the gift to 'es gid hanasheh' and the 580 animals to Se'ir, and explains that the am ha'aretz, rooted in that passuk, sensed that his soul would be returned.

title.en: Lubavitch began the return

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that before Moshiach one tastes of his salvation, and that the process of minchah yashivu was begun by the Rebbes of Lubavitch and continues through the Chabad houses and the thousands of shluchim. He closes with a brachah at the Yud-Tes Kislev melave malka that all Jews merit the full return.

oneLiner.en: On Zos Chanukah the Mashgiach teaches that the mizbe'ach and the Beis HaMikdash stand on unity among Jews, and that forgiving one another brings miracles and the final redemption.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a Zohar on Parshas Mikeitz: Rabbi Abba saw a man saved by two miracles, a snake killed beside him and a ledge that collapsed just after he left it. The man explained that he always forgave those who wronged him and even did them favors, and Rabbi Abba said his deeds were greater than Yosef's. The Mashgiach then turns to the reading of Zos Chanukah and asks why the Torah totals the nesi'im's offerings, which any child could add up. He answers that the mizbe'ach stands on achdus, as the Maharal says; the shared wagons broke down the walls between tribes, and the total shows twelve tribes became one. He brings the Midrash Tanchuma on unity, and the break between Yosef and his brothers that is healed in Vayigash, and prays for the last redemption through such unity. Finally he calls Zos Chanukah a kind of Rosh Hashanah, a day when prayers are answered.

en: In the Zohar, a man who always forgave those who wronged him, and even did them good, merited miracle upon miracle; Rabbi Abba called his deeds greater than Yosef's.
The Torah totals the nesi'im's offerings to show that the mizbe'ach was inaugurated through the unity of all the tribes.
Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach says the Beis HaMikdash stands on achdus, and sinas chinam is why it was destroyed.
When Jews are united, the Midrash Tanchuma says, the attribute of judgment cannot touch them, even if they have sinned gravely.
The Mashgiach prays that, as the earlier exiles ended, the present exile end through Jews forgiving one another wholeheartedly, bringing a second chanukas hamizbe'ach.
Zos Chanukah is a kind of Rosh Hashanah, a day of remembrance and salvation when prayers are accepted.

summary.en: The opening of the shiur.

title.en: Rabbi Abba and the man saved twice

summary.en: The Mashgiach retells a Zohar on Mikeitz: a man sleeping on a mountain ledge near Lod was saved from a snake and from the ledge's collapse, and told Rabbi Abba that he always forgave those who wronged him and did them favors. Rabbi Abba said his deeds were greater than Yosef's and earned him miracle upon miracle; the Mashgiach ties this to Chanukah.

title.en: Why the Torah totals the nesi'im's offerings

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the reading of Zos Chanukah totals what the twelve nesi'im brought, and why it says both 'on the day it was anointed' and 'after it was anointed'. He answers with the Maharal that the mizbe'ach stands on achdus: the shared wagons broke the walls between tribes and the total of a hundred and twenty is a new sum of one united people. He adds the Midrash Tanchuma that judgment cannot touch Jews when they are united.

title.en: Yosef's brothers and the prayer for unity

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Yosef's brothers could not speak peaceably with him because they were men of truth, and shows the repair in Vayigash, where they spoke with him in love. He then prays that the present exile end as the earlier ones did, through Jews forgiving one another wholeheartedly, so that the 'second' chanukas hamizbe'ach, the building of the Beis HaMikdash, will come.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude.

title.en: Zos Chanukah as a Rosh Hashanah of prayer

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Zos Chanukah is a kind of Rosh Hashanah, a day of remembrance like Sarah's, when the barren are remembered and prayers are accepted, and urges using it to pray for every Jew's needs. He then speaks of the treasures of Chanukah, citing the Skverer Rebbe, of Al HaNissim in bentching, and of the Rizhiner's prayer for mercy on the whole world.

title.en: Closing

oneLiner.en: Through a piece of Sfas Emes, the Mashgiach explains that Chanukah opens the source of miracles, a level above nature, so that everything in these days comes through miracles, and he urges using the last day of Chanukah to draw on it.

abstract.en: After a word on the seudos of Chanukah, the Mashgiach turns to a piece of Sfas Emes. It asks why the blessing is 'she'asa nissim' if it refers to the miracle of the oil, and answers that the lighting is not chiefly for that miracle: Chanukah comes from a level above the seven days of nature, the source of miracles, which descends into time during these eight days. As during Sefirah everything relates to the day's sefirah, on Chanukah everything carries miracles; this is why even the first day, with enough oil, has a blessing. The Mashgiach applies this to the last day of Chanukah and to the present need of Jews for miracles, tells of Rabbi Shlomo Kluger and of Ruzhin on the worth of Chanukah, and closes with Chanukah as a time of pekidas akaros, also for one barren in Torah and tefillah.

en: Chanukah comes from a level above nature, the place from which miracles come, and that level descends into the world in these days.
Above the order of nature set in the seven days of creation there is an order of miracles, and on Chanukah it is joined to time.
The blessing 'she'asa nissim' is said not on the miracle of the oil but on the opening of the source of miracles in these days.
Everything on Chanukah, from the food to the candles, carries miracles, and even the first night's light burned from the source of miracles.
The Mashgiach says that on the last day of Chanukah one must work to connect to the source of miracles, since Jews today need miracles.
Chanukah is a time of pekidas akaros, and this includes one who is 'barren' in Torah or in tefillah.

title.en: The seudos of Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the seudos of Chanukah carry some mitzvah because Jews made them, rejoicing that they were moser nefesh for Torah and mitzvos, and he turns to a piece of Sfas Emes.

title.en: Why 'she'asa nissim': the source of miracles

summary.en: Following the Sfas Emes, the Mashgiach asks why the blessing is 'she'asa nissim' if it is for the miracle of the oil, and answers that the lighting is not chiefly for that miracle: Chanukah comes from the level above nature, the order of miracles above the seven days of creation, whose gates open in these days.

title.en: Everything on Chanukah carries miracles

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the eight days join the world of miracles to time. As in Sefirah everything relates to the day's sefirah, on Chanukah, which is hod, everything, even the kugel and the candles, comes from the source of miracles; so the blessing is on the miracles present today, and even the first day, when the oil sufficed, has one.

title.en: The last day and the need for miracles

summary.en: On the last day of Chanukah the Mashgiach says one must strive to connect to the source of miracles, since Hashem has brought Jews, in Eretz Yisroel and elsewhere, to a state where they need miracles. He draws on the Hallel's complaint 'why should the nations say', and notes that tomorrow one can still say Hallel and Al Hanissim.

title.en: Rabbi Shlomo Kluger, Ruzhin and the dreidel

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a question put to Rabbi Shlomo Kluger by a prisoner let out for a short time, and of his answer favoring Hallel with the tzibbur over lighting. He cites the Ruzhiner that a simple Jew can accomplish on Chanukah what a tzaddik accomplishes with his tefillos, and tells of young men playing dreidel and the saying that what one wins on Chanukah cannot be lost.

title.en: Pekidas akaros and closing tefillah

summary.en: After a long niggun, the Mashgiach says Chanukah is a time of pekidas akaros like Rosh Hashanah, and, citing a Midrash, that barrenness includes one who sees no fruit in his Torah or tefillah. He urges using tomorrow's Hallel and Al Hanissim to ask that Jews be remembered with salvation and that barren Zion be remembered, with the ingathering of the exiles.

catalogTitle: The 50th Gate of קדושה is Opposed to the 50th Gate of טומאה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the fiftieth gate of tumah, apikorsus, stands opposite the fiftieth gate of kedushah, emunah, and that the doubts it sends before Moshiach must be ignored rather than argued with.

abstract.en: After a short warning about insects in food during the summer, the Mashgiach turns to Shavuos, the fiftieth day. Hashem took the Jews out of Egypt from the forty-nine gates of tumah just before they fell into the fiftieth, and since everything in creation is balanced, the fifty gates of tumah stand opposite the fifty gates of kedushah. The first forty-nine are midos, each with a nation as its vessel, as he shows with chesed and gevurah and the dream of the Ohr HaChaim; the fiftieth is daas: in kedushah emunah, in tumah apikorsus, whose force is Amalek, numerically equal to safek. Citing the Ohr HaChaim that before Moshiach the Jews fall into this gate, he describes the doubts that torment even believing Jews and explains that they are not logical, so one must ignore them and drive them away, a fulfillment of lo sasuru. He closes with the story of Reb Mendel of Vitebsk and the mazikim.

en: The fifty gates of tumah stand opposite the fifty gates of kedushah, because Hashem made everything in balance.
The first forty-nine gates are midos; the fiftieth is daas: emunah in kedushah and apikorsus in tumah.
Before Moshiach the Jews fall into the fiftieth gate of tumah, and the Torah is what lets them hold on to emunah inside it.
Amalek is the force of the fiftieth gate of tumah; its purpose is to inject doubt in emunah, and Amalek is numerically equal to safek.
Thoughts of doubt are not logical and cannot be answered with logic; one must ignore them and not argue with them.
Driving such a thought away is itself the mitzvah of lo sasuru; the sin is only in giving it lodging in the mind.
The trial is temporary and has a limit; one who fights and stays with emunah comes out with emunah clearer and purer than before.

title.en: Insects in summer; the fiftieth gate

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns about insects in food in the hot weather. He then turns to Shavuos: Hashem took the Jews out of the forty-nine gates of tumah before they fell into the fiftieth, and each day of Sefirah brings them into a gate of kedushah, with the fiftieth being emunah; since everything is balanced, fifty gates of tumah stand opposite fifty gates of kedushah.

title.en: The fiftieth gate is apikorsus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the forty-nine gates are midos while the fiftieth is daas: emunah in kedushah, apikorsus in tumah. He brings the Ohr HaChaim that before Moshiach the Jews will fall into the fiftieth gate; unlike in Egypt they now have the Torah to hold on to, and he says the world today is in that gate.

title.en: The seven nations and the midos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each bad midah has a nation as its vessel. Chesed is giving and gevurah is recoiling; in kedushah the right and the giver lead, as seen in dressing right first and in kiddushin, while in tumah the left dominates, as he shows from Esav and from the Ohr HaChaim's dream of two dogs. That is why the chesed of tumah is called Canaani, and he touches on Chiti for gevurah.

title.en: Amalek and the doubts of today

summary.en: The Mashgiach identifies Amalek as the force of the fiftieth gate of tumah, whose purpose is to inject doubts in emunah. He describes how many believing Jews, even bnei Torah, suffer from such doubts and fight them, and how young men come to him crying, unable to sleep.

title.en: Doubts are not logical

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ruzhiner that before Moshiach simple emunah will be like climbing a slippery wall, and the Zohar on that period. He says even great tzaddikim had such doubts; they are not logical but like a bug, as in people who keep checking a locked door. One of the Erev Rav welcomes such thoughts, while a Jew from Har Sinai fights them; the Mashgiach says not to argue with them, for it is like a fly in a spider web.

title.en: Ignore them: lo sasuru

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a man who could not daven because of an image in his mind, and Rabbi Nachman of Breslov told him to ignore it. Driving such thoughts away is the mitzvah of lo sasuru, and the Mashgiach gives a remez for it. The doubts are a temporary punishment with a limit, and one who fights them comes out with purer emunah.

title.en: Summary: emunah beyond understanding

summary.en: The Mashgiach repeats and summarizes: the fiftieth gate of kedushah, reached on Shavuos, is emunah, which even Moshe Rabbeinu could not grasp, and its opposite is apikorsus, which is also beyond logic. He brings the Chovos HaLevavos's image of ink splashing into a poem, and explains that today, unlike pagan times, people believe in nothing, because this is the time of Amalek, numerically equal to safek.

title.en: A Jew from Sinai resists the doubts

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every Jew who stood at Sinai would give his life for emunah, as whole communities did in the Crusades. The atmosphere is full of apikorsus, so such thoughts penetrate even believers, and he brings the Zohar praising one who holds on to emunah before Moshiach. A Jew from Sinai resents these thoughts while one of the Erev Rav welcomes them; again he says not to argue but to ignore them.

title.en: Reb Mendel of Vitebsk and the mazikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the story the Tzemach Tzedek related: a chassid of Reb Mendel of Vitebsk was taken by mazikim to a bris, warned by a captive woman not to eat, and told by his Rebbe to say they are nothing. The mazikim shrank away as he said it, and Ashmedai told him he had no power over him because his Rebbe's Torah was entirely for Heaven's sake.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, corresponds to Shemini Atzeres and to the ushpiz of Shlomo HaMelech, the moon in its fullness, when holiness conquers the reshus harabim and turns it into a reshus hayachid, in the world and in each Jew's heart.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the menorah standing beside Sukkos: Chanukah, like Sukkos, has eight days, so Zos Chanukah is the counterpart of Shemini Atzeres, whose ushpiz is Shlomo HaMelech. The Chanukah light goes out into the reshus harabim, and holiness breaks into the place and the time of impurity, at the dark end of the month, in Teves. Shlomo, the fifteenth generation from Avraham, is the moon in its fullness; he took the daughters of kings to bring the nations under holiness and strove to bring the days of Moshiach, and even the two harlots, the chief feminine kelipos, submitted to him. Each Jew has his own reshus hayachid and reshus harabim, and Chanukah is the time to subdue the second to the first. After the churban, the festivals no longer gave enough strength for the whole year, so Hashem added Purim and then Chanukah as stations between Sukkos and Pesach. From Chanukah one takes thanksgiving for every small thing. He closes with the mashal of the queen who will return only if the king lifts her up, and a tefilah for Moshiach.

en: Since Chanukah has eight days like Sukkos, Zos Chanukah corresponds to Shemini Atzeres, whose ushpiz is Shlomo HaMelech.
The Chanukah light enters the reshus harabim: holiness conquers both the place and the time that belonged to the other side and turns the public domain into a reshus hayachid.
Shlomo HaMelech is the moon in its fullness, and he took the daughters of kings in order to bring all the nations under holiness.
Every Jew has a reshus hayachid, the side of the heart that longs to serve Hashem, and a reshus harabim that wants only physical things; Chanukah is the time to subdue the second to the first.
After the churban the festivals no longer gave enough strength for the whole year, so Hashem gave Purim and later Chanukah as stations between Sukkos and Pesach.
What one takes from Chanukah is thanksgiving: thanking Hashem constantly, for every small thing.

title.en: Zos Chanukah as Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects the menorah to Sukkos: both festivals have eight days, so Zos Chanukah is the counterpart of Shemini Atzeres, the ushpiz of Shlomo HaMelech. He explains that the Chanukah light goes into the reshus harabim, where holiness conquers the place and the time of the other side, at the dark end of the month and in Teves, breaking in like Peretz.

title.en: Shlomo, the full moon, and his wives

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Shlomo, fifteen generations from Avraham, is the moon in its fullness, and says his ushpiz on Zos Chanukah turns the reshus harabim into a reshus hayachid, with all thirteen attributes of mercy present. He then explains that Shlomo, beloved of Hashem and author of Shir HaShirim, took the daughters of kings for the sake of Heaven, to bring the seventy nations under holiness.

title.en: Shlomo's striving for the days of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Pri Tzaddik that Shlomo tried to bring the days of Moshiach, when Hashem will be King over all the earth, and that in his days the sitra achra submitted to him. The two harlots who came before him were, as the Midrash says, the two chief feminine kelipos, and their submission came through his taking the daughters of kings; this is the power of Zos Chanukah.

title.en: The reshus harabim inside every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew is a small world, with a reshus hayachid in the right side of his heart and a reshus harabim in the left that wants only physical things. Chanukah, and Zos Chanukah above all, is the time to subdue one's reshus harabim so that even physical matters become for the sake of Heaven, as the kingdom of Yavan was handed over to the tzaddikim.

title.en: Purim and Chanukah as stations, and thanksgiving

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the three festivals give strength for the whole year, but after the churban, without the Beis HaMikdash, it was not enough, so Hashem gave Purim and then, against the Greek culture of Yavan, Chanukah, as stations between Sukkos and Pesach. What one takes from Chanukah is thanking Hashem for every small thing, and he tells of an oved who thanked Hashem even over his snuff.

title.en: The king who must lift up the queen

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the holiness of Zos Chanukah comes down to the very lowest place, and brings the passuk 'she has fallen and will no longer rise' as the Gemara in Berachos and the Zohar read it: a king twice sent away the queen and called her back, and the third time she refused to return unless the king himself lifts her up. Every Chanukah reveals the light of Moshiach, and he says one must daven to be lifted and let oneself be lifted. He closes with a tefilah that the light of Moshiach revealed on Chanukah be fulfilled and Moshiach come.
